syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1.  Course description: 
This course introduces the fundamental principles governing aircraft flight, including basic 
aerodynamics, atmospheric properties, aircraft performance, stability and control, propulsion systems, 
and Hypersonic vehicles. Students explore the forces acting on an aircraft and the engineering concepts 
that enable safe and efficient flight. The course provides a foundational understanding of flight 
mechanics and aircraft systems, preparing students for advanced studies in aerospace engineering.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Properties of living systems, Biological macromolecules, Basic physiological processes, 
Genetics, Photosynthesis, Metabolism and Cellular systems. Experiments including but not limited 
to Microscopy, Quantification of Biomolecules, Chlorophyll extraction, Water potential in plant 
tissues and Cell cycle analysis. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
The course is aimed to provide a broad introduction to the major principles and topics in 
biology. The relationship of the living organism with its environment at the molecular level is 
highlighted in line with modern research in biological sciences. By the end of the course, the student 
would have gained an overall understanding of the essential aspects of biology – both as a basic 
science and as a branch with wide-ranging applications in industry, medicine and human health. It 
is also expected that using the acquired knowledge, he/she would be able to devise/suggest strategies 
to solve some of the  imminent problems faced by mankind and the world at large through 
technological solutions. Students shall also get hands -on experience on fundamental aspects of 
practical biology.

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: This course is intended to offer an introduction to the world of Biological 
Chemistry. The course deals with the structure, properties, and significance of the major groups of 
biochemical compounds (amino acids, proteins, carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and lipids), the 
bioenergetics, enzyme mechanisms and regulation of the central metabolic pathways. Efforts will 
be made to include the recent advances and methodologies related to biochemistry. This would 
help students going for higher level activities, appreciation of biochemical problems, eva luation 
and problem solving. 
2.  Text Book (TB):  Mary K. Campbell and Shawn O. Farrell, Biochemistry, 9th 
edition, International edition, copyright 2018 (Thompson Brooks/Cole, Cengage 
Learning) 
3.         Reference Books (RB): a) D. Nelson & M Cox. Lehninger, Principles of 
Biochemistry, Palgrave, 4th Ed. b) Donald Voet et al., Biochemistry, Wiley. 
Other teaching resource/material may also be used which will be shared by instructors.

makeup.heading: Make-up policy

sources.text:
Make-up policy: If a student misses the Mid -Semester or Comprehensive Examination due to a genuine 
reason (serious medical causes leading to hospitalization (certified by doctor from BITS medical center), 
personal/family emergencies) there exists a provision to apply for make -up. Prior permission must be taken 
from the Instructor-in-Charge, before applying for make -up. Make-up decisions will be  made on a case -by-
case basis and only genuine cases as determined by the Departmental team will be considered. No Make -Up 
will be granted for quiz, assignments and Lab components.  
Grading Policy: Award of grades would be guided by the histogram of marks and course average. "If a 
student obtains below 30% of the average of the top three performers or 40% of median, whichever is lower, 
the student will not be awarded a valid grade and the case will be reported as “NC”."

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
The course deals with theoretical aspects and selected experiments of recombinant DNA manipulation. 
Emphasis will be placed on procedures to create chimeric molecules using examples from actual experimental 
work. Vector designing, PCR, DNA sequencing, in vitro mutagenesis, cloning in prokaryotic and eukaryotic 
systems and whole genome approaches will be covered. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the course: 
Almost every field of modern experimental biology relies heavily on DNA manipulation techniques.  This 
course will expose the student to the foundations and principles underlying such molecular biology methods 
and give a brief yet broad overview of the recent trends and applications of recombinant DNA technology. 
 
3. Text Book (TB): 
Howe, Christopher J. Gene Cloning and Manipulation (2nd edition). New Delhi: Cambridge University Press 
India Pvt. Ltd., 2015. 
 
4. Reference Books (RB): 
• RBa: Brown, Terence A. Gene Cloning and DNA Analysis: An Introduction (8 th edition). United 
Kingdom: Wiley-Blackwell, 2010.  
• RBb: Primrose, Sandy B. and Richard Twyman. Principles of Gene Manipulation and Genomics (7th  
edition). New York: Blackwell Science, 2006.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Biomolecular Conformations, Structural genomics and proteomics, protein folding, 
Forcefield, Simulation, Conformational analysis, ab initio structure prediction, comparative modeling, lattice 
models, usage of modeling packages. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  The course is designed to provide students the firsthand experience 
of potential utility of biomolecular modeling especially in concurrent pharmaceutical research, and in cell and 
structural biology. It d escribes the functionality, advantages, and limitations of standard co mputing 
strategies for the simulation of biomolecules. Provide a working knowledge of freely available software to 
carry out independent research projects in biomolecular modeling and explore the possibilities for modeling 
to assist in the process of determination, analyzing, evaluating, displaying, and retrieving of 3D structure data 
in a research or industry laboratory environment.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
Enzyme nomenclature and classification; isolation and purification; structures; kinetics; regulation of 
enzymatic reactions; evaluation of enzymes and other proteins. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This course is designed to provide a broad introduction about enzymes, including their isolation, 
purification, structure and kinetics. Efforts will be made to understand the molecular basis of how enzymes 
catalyze the biological and non-natural reactions. Emphasis will be given to study the practical and 
industrial application of enzymes. This course integrates basics as well as current advances in enzymology 
and will create research interest among the students.

cell antigen recognition and activation. Immunity to microbes and diseases caused b y humoral 
and cell mediated immune responses will be covered and emphasis placed on congenital and 
acquired immuno-deficiencies. Advanced topics like antibody engineering will be discussed with 
the help of review articles.

names: Study of molecular diversity of microorganisms
Stahl D.A. . Brock Biology of Microorganism

sources.text:
Lab instructor : Juhi Mishra, Jennifer  
 
1. Course of Description: Molecular taxonomy, Systematic Microbiology, Study of molecular 
diversity of microorganisms, Molecular tools employed in the study of microbial ecology, clinical 
microbiology, human -microbe interaction, molecular plant -microbe interaction, applied 
microbiology, and synthetic microbiology.  
2. Scope & Objective of the Course: 
This course deals with an in -depth study of microbial taxonomy and evolution,  as well as the 
molecular aspects  of microbe -host interactions. In addition, it includes applied aspects of 
microorganisms being utilized in industry and human health . It also emphasize s on recent 
development in microbial genomics, nanotechnology and biotechnology.  
 
3. Text Book (TB):  
Madigan M.T., Martinko J.M., Bender K.S., Buckley D.H., Stahl D.A. (2017). Brock Biology of 
Microorganism, 14th Ed., Pearson International Education   
 
4. Reference Book (RB): 
 1. Wiley, J.M., Sherwood, L.M., Woolverton, C.J. (2007). Prescott, Harley, and Klein’s 
Microbiology, 7th Ed. McGraw-Hill International Edition. 
2. Glazer, A.N. and Nikaido, H. (2008).  Microbial Biotechnology, Fundamentals of Applied 
Microbiology, 2nd Ed., Cambridge.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
Animal cell and tissue culture techniques from various organisms, basics of primary cell culture, types of cell 
lines, generation and maintenance of cell lines, current advanced technology for cell biology application, 
manipulation and applications of cell culture technology for Biotechnological research and its therapeutic 
application. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
 
In this course we will discuss: 
 Biology of cultured cells & cell microenvironment 
 Maintenance, culture cryopreservation and Quantitation of cells 
 Primary cultures and cell lines 
 Cytotoxicity, proliferation and Cell Transformation 
 Cellular Imaging Techniques and its application  
 Scaling up and Automation.

wastes. Ethical issues related with the release of genetically modified organism.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Biostatistics and Biomodeling course has two components. Biostatistics  
part will provide an introduction to the basic concepts of statistical methods to equip students 
with statistical reasoning in their fields of study. Topics include variables in biology, Standard 
deviation; correlation and regression analysis; significance tests; chi square, t -test, ANOVA 
etc. Emphasis is placed on the application of fundamental concepts to real world situations. 
Biomodeling is designed to provide students the first -hand experience of modelling 
biomolecules to elucidate the relationships between sequence, structure and function. 
Specifically, different computing strategies for the simulation of biomolecules will be  
discussed with regard to their utility, advantages, and limitations. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The student would learn how to collect data suitable for 
statistical analyses, unde rstand the general features of the data collected, making statistical 
inferences and likelihood of occurrence of an event using probability calculations and tests of 
significance.

makeup.heading: Make-up Policy

sources.text:
10. Make-up Policy: 
If a student misses the Mid-Semester or Comprehensive Examination due to a genuine reason (serious 
medical causes leading to hospitalization (certified by doctor from BITS medical center), 
personal/family emergencies) there exists a provision to apply for make-up. Prior permission must 
be taken from the Instructor-in-Charge, before applying for make-up. Make-up decisions will 
be made on a case-by-case basis and only genuine cases as determined by the Departmental team will 
be considered. No Make-Up will be granted for quiz and assignments.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Properties of living systems, Biological macromolecules, Basic physiological processes, 
Genetics, Photosynthesis, Metabolism and Cellular systems. Experiments including but not limited 
to Microscopy, Quantification of Biomolecules, Chlorophyll extraction, Water potential in plant 
tissues and Cell cycle analysis. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
The course is aimed to provide a broad introduction to the major principles and topics in 
biology. The relationship of the living organism with its environment at the molecular level is 
highlighted in line with modern research in biological sciences. By the end of the course, the student 
would have gained an overall understanding of the essential aspects of biology – both as a basic 
science and as a branch with wide-ranging applications in industry, medicine and human health. It 
is also expected that using the acquired knowledge, he/she would be able to devise/suggest strategies 
to solve some of the  imminent problems faced by mankind and the world at large through 
technological solutions. Students shall also get hands -on experience on fundamental aspects of 
practical biology.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
Enzyme nomenclature and classification; isolation and purification; structures; kinetics; regulation of 
enzymatic reactions; evaluation of enzymes and other proteins. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This course is designed to provide a broad introduction about enzymes, including their isolation, 
purification, structure and kinetics. Efforts will be made to understand the molecular basis of how enzymes 
catalyze the biological and non-natural reactions. Emphasis will be given to study the practical and 
industrial application of enzymes. This course integrates basics as well as current advances in enzymology 
and will create research interest among the students.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: The food sector is very important from the economical point of view, and is 
one of the industrial areas where Biotechnology has played and still plays a pivotal role. In this course, 
a general view of the basic aspects (physical-chemical aspects, structure, spoilage), of foods and their 
processing and preservation techniques will be taught. Further the most relevant aspects for a future 
biotechnologist in the food industry will be studied: role of microorganisms and enzymes for the 
production and transformation of foods and most recent advances in foods made of/with genetically 
modified organisms. In addition, food safety and quality management along with food waste 
management will be covered. Finally, case studies of successful entrepre neurship ventures in Food 
Biotechnology will be discussed. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  The aim of this course is providing the students with basic 
knowledge about the applications of Biotechnology in the food industry and in food -related sectors. 
These include the preservation tools used, production of recombinant proteins and additives to use in 
food technology, transgenic foods, diagnostic system used in food industry  including advanced 
techniques like biosensors and artificial intelligence, and ethics and safety of food biotechnology.

2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  The aim of this course is providing the students with basic 
knowledge about the applications of Biotechnology in the food industry and in food -related sectors. 
These include the preservation tools used, production of recombinant proteins and additives to use in 
food technology, transgenic foods, diagnostic system used in food industry  including advanced 
techniques like biosensors and artificial intelligence, and ethics and safety of food biotechnology.

syllabus.text:
The food sector is very important from the economical point of view, and is 
one of the industrial areas where Biotechnology has played and still plays a pivotal role. In this course, 
a general view of the basic aspects (physical-chemical aspects, structure, spoilage), of foods and their 
processing and preservation techniques will be taught. Further the most relevant aspects for a future 
biotechnologist in the food industry will be studied: role of microorganisms and enzymes for the 
production and transformation of foods and most recent advances in foods made of/with genetically 
modified organisms. In addition, food safety and quality management along with food waste 
management will be covered. Finally, case studies of successful entrepre neurship ventures in Food 
Biotechnology will be discussed.

food technology, transgenic foods, diagnostic system used in food industry  including advanced 
techniques like biosensors and artificial intelligence, and ethics and safety of food biotechnology.

sources.text:
1. Course Description: In this course students will be assigned study work in advanced areas of professional 
interest. Each student will work under the overall supervision and guidance of a faculty member and will  in  
the end submit a project report encompassing critical review of the material studied. 
The organization and evaluation of the course would be achieved through seminars, group discussions, project 
report etc. The course will be conducted by the team of teachers who provide guidance for study work. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The course aims at covering topics in advanced areas of professional 
interest and will be conducted on self -study and seminar basis. The course is specially designed to provide an 
opportunity to the students for developme nt of their academic skills and logical thinking through open ended 
advanced study oriented activities. As a part of education, this course follows a method of learning and, 
therefore, the student's actual day -to-day task involvement would constitute the c entral thread of the learning 
process. The evaluation will recognize this aspect by demanding day -to-day productivity, punctuality and final 
achievement of the student. 
3. Operation of the course: 
The plan of work for each student will be decided by the respe ctive Instructors/supervisors. Each student 
should adhere to the plan of work decided for and should regularly monitor the progress of the course 
accordingly. The final report encompassing critical review of the material studied will be submitted to the 
Instructor-in-charge through Departmental Committee on Academics (DCA) by the end of the class work.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
The course includes fundamentals and techniques of technical drawing and standard practices of 
the same so that design ideas can be adequately communicated and produced. It introduces students 
to the theories of projection and the concepts of engineering drawing using the most widely used 
CAD application software, AutoCAD. Basic AutoCAD 2023 commands will also be introduced. The 
course covers the following topics: Introduction to AutoCAD basic commands; theory of projections; 
orthographic projections; isometric projections; projection of points, lines, planes and solids; section 
of solids; developments of surfaces. 
 
2. Scope and objective of the course: 
Computerized drafting provides accurate and easily modifiable graphics entities, easy data storage 
and retrieval facility and enhances creativity. 
Upon successful completion of this course, the student will be able to: 
 Read and interpret engineering drawings 
 Identify the three principal projection planes 
 Draw 2-dimensional orthographic projections from given 3-dimensional views 
 Create an isometric drawing using AutoCAD 
 Comprehend orthographic and multiview projection 
 Apply the concept of cutting planes to create the various types of sectional views 
 Become conversant with appropriate use of AutoCAD software for drafting.

syllabus.heading: Course Plan

sources.text:
6. Course Plan 
Module 1: Basic Concepts and Definitions  
Learning Objectives 
• To define the terminologies and associated basic concepts of thermodynamics such as system, 
state, state postulate, equilibrium, process, and  cycle. 
• To review concepts of temperature, temperature scales, pressure, and absolute and gauge 
pressure. 
 
Lecture 
No. 
Topics to be covered  Text book 
Chap/Sec # 
1-3 Introduction, thermodynamic systems  and control volume, properties & 
state, process & cycle, force, energy, pressure, specific volume, zeroth law.  
1 
 
 
Module 2: Properties of Pure Substances  
Learning Objectives 
• To introduce the concept of a pure substance and discuss the physics of phase change 
processes. 
• To illustrate the P-v, T-v, and P-T property diagrams and P-v-T surfaces of pure substances. 
• To determine thermodynamic properties of pure substances and ideal gases from tables of 
property data and charts. 
 
Lecture 
No. 
Topics to be covered  Text book 
Chap/Sec # 
4-7 Pure substance, Phase equilibrium, Independent properties, Tables of 
thermodynamic properties & their use  
2 
8-9 P-V-T behavior, Compressibility factor, Equation of state  2 
 
Module 3: Energy Transfer  
Learning Objectives 
• To introduce and define the concept of heat and work for correct analysis of thermodynamics 
systems. 
• To learn and determine different kinds of work like moving boundary work or PdV work 
commonly encountered in reciprocating devices such as automotive engines and 
compressors, electric work,  etc. 
 
Lecture 
No. 
Text book Chap/Sec #  Text book 
Chap/Sec # 
10-11 Definition of work and its identification, work done at the moving boundary  
Concept of heat, comparison of heat and work, Engineering Applications  
3

continuity, Differentiation, Integration, Application of derivatives and definite integration.

Instructor-in-charge : Prof. Natasha Hazarika 
 
1. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course is designed to provide students with a 
comprehensive understanding of how science and technology interact with societal structures, 
economic systems, and global governance. The course begins with an introduction to 
foundational perspectives on technological change and scientific knowledge systems, offering a 
basic orientation to how technologies are developed and adopted. It then moves to the 
examination of Intellectual Property Rights and Innovation, focusing on real -world issues such 
as patent disputes, corporate competition, and the strategic control of innovation. The third and 
final module explores Science, Technology, and Social Stratification, encouraging students to 
consider how power, inequality, and institutional interests influence technological priorities and 
outcomes. Overall, it critically assesses the societal responsibilities and consequences of 
scientific and technological work in contemporary settings.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Linear equations and matrices, Determinants, Basis of Rn , Eigen Value, Eigen 
Vector, Linear transformations on Rn . Linear Programming: Geometric Solutions, Simplex Method, 
Duality, Post optimal Analysis, Transportation and Assignment Problem. Nonlinear Programming 
(Unconstrained optimization). 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
The course is made for Pharmacy students keeping in mind the importance of Linear Algebra and Linear 
programming problems and their possible applications in various fields of science and engineering. Linear 
algebra begins with vectors and matrices – two of  the most important practical concepts in mathematics. 
Whereas Linear programming is a method to achieve the best outcome in a mathematical model whose 
requirements are represented by linear relationships. Linear programming can be applied to various field s of 
study. It is used in business and economics, but can also be utilized for some engineering problems. Industries 
that use linear programming models include transportation, energy, telecommunications, and manufacturing.

sources.text:
1. Course description: Basic concepts related to heat transfer, mass transfer and flow of  fluid, 
processes and equipment involved in extraction and filtration; mixing and granulation; size reduction 
and classification, evaporation and distillation, drying and crystallization, humidification and 
dehumidification. Materials of construction. Theory of compression and consolidation of solids.

syllabus.heading: Course Plan

sources.text:
5. Course Plan: weekly schedule for 14 weeks with [3] lectures per week 
Lectures  
 
Lecture session/Tutorial 
Session Reference Learning objectives 
1 Introduction to process 
engineering 
[Class 
notes] 
To understand the importance of different unit 
operations in pharmaceutical formulation 
development 
2-4 
Basics of flow of fluids, 
heat transfer and mass 
transfer 
[RB1 §§ 11-
13] 
To understand basic principle involved in the flow of 
fluids, heat transfer and mass transfer 
5-7 Size Reduction [TB2 §10] 
To understand the principle, construction and 
working of different mills used in the 
pharmaceutical industry 
8-9 Size Separation [TB2 §10] 
To study the different method of size separation 
including sieving, microscopy, sedimentation and 
coulter counter, To understand the criteria of 
selection of suitable separation method 
10-11 Particle size analysis [TB2 §9] 
To determine the particle size of the powder blend, 
presentation and interpretation of particle size 
data.  
12-14 Evaporation [RB1 §10] 
To understand principles, construction, working, 
uses, merits and demerits of Steam jacketed kettle, 
horizontal tube evaporator, climbing film 
evaporator, forced circulation evaporator, multiple 
effect evaporator& Economy of multiple effect 
evaporator. 
15-17 Distillation [RB1 §23] 
To study basic principles and methodology of simple 
distillation, flash distillation, fractional distillation, 
distillation under reduced pressure, steam 
distillation & molecular distillation 
18-20 Drying [TB1 §3] 
To understand mechanism of drying and to study 
principles , construction, working, uses, merits and 
demerits of Tray dryer, drum dryer spray 
dryer, fluidized bed dryer, vacuum dryer, freeze 
dryer.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  Environment, human population, and industrialization; natural resources and the 
impact of man-made activities on them; structure and function of ecosystem, population ecology, biodiversity 
and its conservation, environmental pollution, social issues and t he environment, and environmental impact 
assessment. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development 
(UNCED) held in Rio De Janero in 1992, the 1994 conference on United Nations Framework Convention on 
Climate Change (UNFCCC), and a very recent 2015 Paris Agreement have created awareness among the 
people around the globe about the deteriorating condition of Earth’s environment. It has warned us not to be 
ignorant of the environmental issues.  In lieu of the  situation, the Hon’ble Supreme Court directed the UGC 
to introduce a basic course on environment for undergraduate students in India. 
The course is designed to cover all aspects of environment [Ecological including biotic (flora - fauna) and 
abiotic (air, water, soil & geography), social, economic and aesthetical]. The course is of interdisciplinary 
nature dealing with social, biological & engineering aspects of environment. The role of biotic and abiotic 
factors in the functioning of the environment, the i mpact of anthropogenic activities on the environment, 
different environmental pollutants, its impact and management strategies; and ecological, socio -political and 
economic issues will be discussed with appropriate real-life examples and case studies. The course would also 
provide insight into practical solutions to different environmental issues. Finally, important concepts of 
environmental impact assessment from all the above mentioned sources would be dealt with. The interested 
students can take the lear nings forward from this point and enrich themselves further by doing other 
electives/projects in these areas.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:
Algorithm Analysis – Mathematical preliminaries, Sorting Algorithms, Search Algorithms, Linear
Structures, Non-Linear Structures, Hashing, Graphs and Algorithms.
(Open elective for non-B.E. Computer Science students)
2. Scope & Objective of the Course:
A data structure is a way to organize large amounts of data, their relationships, and the opera-
tions that can be applied to them. This course focuses on applying data structures like stacks,
queues, linked lists, heaps, trees, and graphs, along with algorithmic techniques such as brute-
force, greedy, divide-and- conquer, and dynamic programming, to solve real-world problems, in-
cluding shortest paths in maps, spell checking, and social network analysis.
Objectives
•Apply basic data structures (stacks, queues, linked lists, trees) to solve programming prob-
lems.
•Implement advanced data structures (graphs, balanced search trees, hash tables, priority
queues) for complex applications.
•Use algorithmic techniques (brute-force, greedy, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming)
to address real-world challenges.
•Develop skills to design and implement data abstractions for problem-solving.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
This course provides students with a foundation in engineering design practice and prepares them for discipline-specific 
advanced courses in engineering design. Students will gain experience in the use of digital design techniques and 
management of larger open -ended, team -based engineering design tasks in a project -based learning environment. 
Students will learn to create detailed designs of real -world products and systems by applying design thinking and 
scientific principles. Students will learn a range of design techniques to contextualize, evaluate, and communicate 
designs, from generating ideas via sketching to development of digital models and detailed technical drawings that meet 
the international standards. Students will develop foundation skills in computer -aided design (CAD) techniques to 
generate 3D models of products and assemblies and learn to integrate them in augmented and virtual reality tools.

syllabus.heading: COURSE DESCRIPTION

sources.text:
1. COURSE DESCRIPTION 
This course introduces the fundamental concepts and analytical tools of game theory for studying strategic interactions 
among rational decision -makers. It covers the construction and classification of games with complete and incomplete 
Information, strategic behavior, and solution concepts, including dominant strategy equilibrium, iterated elimination of 
strictly dominated strategies (IESDS), Nash equilibrium, mixed strategy equilibrium, and static and dynamic games with 
and without complete Information. It also includes extensive-form games, finite- and infinitely-repeated games, Bayesian 
games, and the integration of linear programming with game -theoretic analysis. Emphasis is placed on applications to 
economics and public policy, including social choice and voting theory, trade, environmental economics, industrial  
organization, auctions, negotiations, and other strategic decision-making problems. 
 
2. SCOPE AND OBJECTIVE OF THE COURSE 
Game Theory is a tool and is a beautiful mix of mathematics, economics, and psychology. Game theory is a technique for 
analyzing strategic problems across diverse settings. The foundation of Game Theory was laid by John von Neumann, who 
proved the fundamental minimax theorem in 1928 and published a book (co-authored with Oskar Morgenstern), Theory of 
Games and Economic Behavior, in 1944. Game Theory became a buzzword and attained particular glamour, with the Nobel 
Prize going to John Nash for his contributions to the Field , which has found applications in almost every branch of 
knowledge. Broadly, Game Theory can be divided into cooperative and non -cooperative game theory. Th is course deals 
only with non-cooperative games. The main objective is to introduce students to Game Theory & Its applications to the real 
world as a tool for logical thinking in a strategic interaction setting.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to artificial intelligence techniques for robotic systems with 
emphasis on adaptive learning, machine learning, and cognitive decision making. Topics include: Evolution of 
intelligent robotics; adaptive learning algorithms; biologically inspired learning using Dynamic Hebbian Learning 
and adaptive oscillators; statistical learning and adaptive estimation; data -driven modelling of serial -chain 
manipulator kinematics using neural networks; reinforcement learning for robot trajectory planning and decision 
making; and high -level robot co ntrol through large language models/vision language models (using camera 
sensors). Each module contains hands -on sessions and project -based learning to emphasize implementation of 
intelligent algorithms for adaptation, learning, and autonomous algorithm for robotics. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This course introduces the fundamental concepts of Artificial Intelligence for Robotics through the lens of 
adaptive, data-driven, and cognitive robotic systems. Unlike conventional robotics courses that prim arily focus on 
analytical modelling and control, this course emphasizes how robots can learn, adapt, and make intelligent 
decisions using modern AI techniques while remaining grounded in classical robotics principles. 
Students will explore multiple paradigms of robot intelligence, ranging from adaptive learning algorithms and 
biologically inspired learning mechanisms to neural networks, reinforcement learning, and high -level cognitive 
reasoning using vision and large language models. Through hands -on experiments, students will investigate how 
intelligent algorithms can be applied to serial -chain robotic manipulators for learning kinematics, trajectory 
generation, sensor adaptation, and autonomous task execution. 
Course Outcome: 
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: 
CO1 Explain and compare adaptive, statistical, machine learning, and AI -based approaches for developing 
intelligent robotic systems. 
CO2 Develop and implement adaptive learning algorithms, including Dynamic Hebbian Learning and statistical 
learning methods, for robotic sensing, adaptation, and motion generation. 
CO3 Design and evaluate neural network and reinforcement learning approaches for solving robot kinematics 
and trajectory planning problems in serial-chain manipulators. 
CO4 Develop AI -enabled robotic applications that integrate vision to generate high -level task commands for 
autonomous robotic manipulation.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Introduction to HCI in the AI era; Understanding People: Perception, Motor control, 
Cognition, Needs, and Experience; User Research: Interviews, Field research, and Survey research; 
Understanding Interaction: Usability Engineering, Information and control, Dialogue, Tool use, Automation, 
and Rationality; User Interfaces: Input devices, Displays, Interaction techniques, and Reality -based 
interaction; Design: Cognition, Practice, and Processes; Engineering: Systems, Design engineering, Safety 
and risk, and Co mputational representations and models; Evaluation: Analytical methods, Think -aloud 
studies, and Experiment. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: At the completion of this course, students will be able to: 
 
• Understand the concepts and theories of human-AI interaction. Furthermore, they will be able to 
explain basic concepts from the relevant theories in cognitive and social sciences. (LO1)  
• Illustrate and compare methods of “user-centered engineering (UCE)”, involving future users in 
various stages of the design and development process of AI systems. (LO2)  
• Apply “user-centered” methods appropriately, as a team; as part of design, development, and 
evaluation of AI systems. (LO3)  
• Apply ethics procedures for user studies (e.g., privacy, consent) and FATE principles in design of 
prototype based AI systems. (LO4)  
• Describe the perspectives and values of multiple stakeholders at different stages of the user-centered 
engineering process (requirements, design, and evaluation). (LO5)  
 
3. Textbook (T1): Hornbæk, Kasper, Per Ola Kristensson, and Antti Oulasvirta, Introduction to Human-
Computer Interaction (HCI) (Oxford, 2025; online edn, Oxford Academic, 21 Aug. 2025), 
https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780192864543.001.0001 - Open Access) 
4. Reference Book (R1): Human – Centered AI (HCAI) by Ben Shneiderman, 2022 (Available via BITS 
Library) & Research Papers (RP)

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Introduction to Gender Studies and Feminist Movements; Theories of Gender; 
Sex, Gender and Sexuality; Social Construction of Gender; Intersectionality and Social Location; 
Marriage, Family and Gender Discrimination; Gender and Labour Politics; Productivity and Labour 
Issues; Unpaid Domestic Work and Gendered Labour; Globalization, Global Assembly Line, Care 
Work and Emotion Labour; Ideal Worker Norm and Second Shift; Gender Discrimination in the 
Workplace; Media Representations and Male Gaze; Theories of Masculinity; Gender Based Violence. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: To develop the knowledge necessary for addressing issues of 
gender equity and understanding gender roles. The course would help students get a greater insight 
into women’s rights, their role in shaping political, social, economic and cultural institutions. 
Emphasis would be laid on understanding the dynamics of gender relations in educational institutions, 
work and home. The course would further aim at gender sensitization in the context of societal 
stratifications.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:
Micro electro mechanical systems (MEMS), devices and technologies. Micro-machining and mi-
crofabrication techniques. Transduction mechanisms and modeling in different energy domains.
Analysis of micromachined capacitive, piezoresistive and thermal sensors/actuators and applica-
tions. Computer- aided design for MEMS layout, fabrication and analysis.
2. Scope & Objective of the Course:
The course introduces the basic concepts in MEMS (Micro Electromechanical Systems) with a
view to address a class of students from science and engineering disciplines. The discussion
on topics like MEMS design, Microfabrication, Microfluidics, Sensors and actuators have been
structured in the course plan. The objective of the course is to equip the students from various
aspects and with basic knowledge of the area of MEMS.

Course Title : Introduction to Nano Science

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1.Course Description:
Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address  
critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This  
course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and  
nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this 
rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, 
their synthesis and properties of nanomaterials, with emphasis on their size-dependent  
physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials 
in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will 
be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to 
nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and 
future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered.
2.Scope and Objective of the Course:
The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview  
of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis 
of nanoparticles and nanostructures.
Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials  
and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights 
real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological  
domains.
This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical  
exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into  
advanced study or research in the field.

Scope and Objective of the Course:

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
This course provides an introduction to nanotechnology, emphasizing its applications in renewable energy and 
environmental engineering. It covers fundamental concepts, including the distinction between the macro - and 
nanoscale, nanoscale phenomena, and the distinctive properties of nanomaterials that enable them to outperform 
many conventional materials. The course also discusses the fundamentals of fabrication, characterization, and 
operating principles of advanced energy devices, including organic, quantum dot, and dye-sensitized solar cells, 
fuel cells, batteries, and carbo n nanotube-based energy storage systems , and the application of nanomaterials 
for hydrogen production and storage. In addition, it examines the application of nanotechnology in improving 
solar cells, nanoelectrodes, nanocoating, catalyst materials for fuel cells, and battery technologies. The course 
further explores the role of nanotechnology in environmental sustainability, including groundwater remediation, 
nanoadsorbents, ecotoxicology, nanomaterial toxicity, transport and fate of nanomaterials in the en vironment, 
and the broader societal impacts of nanotechnology. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative technology with the potential to significantly benefit 
society across diverse fields. This course is de signed to equip students with the fundamental knowledge and 
skills required for advanced academic research or industrial careers in nanotechnology, with particular 
emphasis on applications in renewable energy and environmental sustainability.  The course is divided into 3 
modules as decribed below. 
o Module 1: General introduction to principles of nanoscience and technology 
o Module 2: Nanotechnology applications in the renewable energy sector 
o Module 3: Nanotechnology applications in the environmental sector. 
The specific topics covered under each module are listed in the course plan (refer to section 6 of this handout).

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
This course provides an introduction to nanotechnology, emphasizing its applications in renewable energy and 
environmental engineering. It covers fundamental concepts, including the distinction between the macro - and 
nanoscale, nanoscale phenomena, and the distinctive properties of nanomaterials that enable them to outperform 
many conventional materials. The course also discusses the fundamentals of fabrication, characterization, and 
operating principles of advanced energy devices, including organic, quantum dot, and dye-sensitized solar cells, 
fuel cells, batteries, and carbo n nanotube-based energy storage systems , and the application of nanomaterials 
for hydrogen production and storage. In addition, it examines the application of nanotechnology in improving 
solar cells, nanoelectrodes, nanocoating, catalyst materials for fuel cells, and battery technologies. The course 
further explores the role of nanotechnology in environmental sustainability, including groundwater remediation, 
nanoadsorbents, ecotoxicology, nanomaterial toxicity, transport and fate of nanomaterials in the en vironment, 
and the broader societal impacts of nanotechnology. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative technology with the potential to significantly benefit 
society across diverse fields. This course is de signed to equip students with the fundamental knowledge and 
skills required for advanced academic research or industrial careers in nanotechnology, with particular 
emphasis on applications in renewable energy and environmental sustainability.  The course is divided into 3 
modules as decribed below. 
o Module 1: General introduction to principles of nanoscience and technology 
o Module 2: Nanotechnology applications in the renewable energy sector 
o Module 3: Nanotechnology applications in the environmental sector. 
The specific topics covered under each module are listed in the course plan (refer to section 6 of this handout).

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:
This is a ﬁrst course on Pattern recognition. It begins with an introduction to the fundamentals of
digital images and develops the theoretical background for the pattern recognition. It goes on to
discuss the different aspects like the preprocessing of a digital image, segmentation, representation
and description and ﬁnally the object recognition. During the course, a ﬂavour of matlab programming
will also be given.
2. Scope & Objective of the Course:
Over the past 30 years or so, pattern recognition and automation have evolved into a mature subject
embracing many topics and applications: these range from automatic (robot) assembly to automatic
vehicle guidance, from automatic interpretation of documents to veriﬁcation of signatures, and from
analysis of remotely sensed images to checking of ﬁngerprints and human blood cells. Currently,
pattern recognition and automatic visual inspection are undergoing very substantial growth, neces-
sary improvement in quality, safety and cost effectiveness being the stimulating factors. The course
introduces the students to the fundamentals of digital images and various processing techniques that
are applied to them not only to improve their quality but also to recognize them.

one of the two criteria: 20% of the median of the post-comprehensive examination score OR 20% 
of the average of the first three top scorers. The lower value between these two criteria will be 
considered as passing marks in this course. NC may also be awarded if a student misses 
regular evaluation components (except lecture surprise tests) even if he/she satisfies the above 
criteria.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
Course Description: 
Introduction of renewable energy, advantages, potential, status of development, broad details of 
different renewable energy systems such as solar, wind, biomass, microhydel, geothermal etc; 
Renewable energy development policy, Renewable energy industries, international co-operation, 
HRD and career growth opportunities, consultancy areas and future thrust areas in renewable 
energy development.

sources.text:
Instructor In Charge           : Ankan Pal (ankan.pal@pilani.bits-pilani.ac.in) 
 
Description: This course is an introduction to the basic theory and practice of cryptographic techniques 
used in information security. The course is intended to understand the mathematical concepts used for 
designing cryptosystems. The focus would be on the mathematical concepts from Number Theory and 
Abstract Algebra. We will delve into  topics such as encryption ( private-key and public -key), digital 
signatures, user authentication, key management, cryptographic hashing, Network security protocols, 
public-key infrastructure, digital rights management, and advancement in mode rn cryptology such as 
Identity Based Encryption, Steganography and Watermarking, Post-Quantum Cryptography, and Zero-
Knowledge protocols.

Instructor-in-Charge : R. MAHESH 
 
 
1. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
 
This course is designed to create an awareness on the basic concepts of biosafety and bioethics that are 
essential for various branches of science which has had an great impact on quality of life and regulations 
governing the experimentations on transgenic organisms and plants, prenatal diagnosis and related social 
issues, handling and disposal of hazardous materials, environmental pollution concerns and ethics in need 
based experimentation on animals and plants, would be  addressed. Emphasis will also be made on health 
care related issues.

genetic testing

CPSEA guidelines 31-34  TB:4.3, 5.1-5.2; 
RB-2:13-15

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are 
expected to create a technology product -based or s ervice/SaaS-based startup and complete the business 
model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture.  
In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases 
of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3) 
go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations  and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on 
customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive 
analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guest-
lectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running 
Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide 
them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded.  The top teams may be 
invited to compete for  seed funding in early 202 7 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the 
completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business.  
2. Scope & Objective of the Course:  
NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence, 
the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC 
helps them to think and act entrepreneurially.  The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform 
an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a 
reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific 
market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build 
an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win 
customers? How wil l your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key 
external partners?

analysis methodologies; mitigation of environmental impacts; case studies; environmental 
management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: This is a course dealing with an advanced pursuit in terms of a study or a lab project 
in assigned area of professional interest. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  Each student will work under the overall supervision and guidance 
of an assigned teacher. The course must end with a well-defined project report outlining, all the investigative 
efforts and conclusions. 
3. Operation of the course:  
1. Within 2 weeks of registration, the student should prepare the work plan for his/her research project 
and also for the developmental activities in consultation with the supervisor. 
2. Mid semester grading will be done by the supervisor based on the work done and progress made 
towards planned objectives by the student in the assigned research area. The student is required to 
submit mid semester report describing the work done and progress made by him/her. He/she should 
also deliver a seminar to highlight these activities. Supervisor will grade the student for mid semester 
on the basis of the mid semester report described above and the Seminar presented by the student. 
3. The student should submit mid-semester report in the 9th week of the semester to the supervisor and 
this should be followed by seminar/presentation by the student. The supervisor in turn is required to 
send mid-semester grades of all the students working with him to Instructor -in-charge by the end of 
9th week of the semester. 
4. End semester report would provide details of work done by the student. End semester report should be 
submitted to the supervisor and should be followed by seminar/presentation.

1. Aims and Objectives 
This course is designed to train the students towards acquiring competence in research 
methodologies. The course will be conducted in terms of actual participation in Research and 
Development Work . Each student will be assigned to a faculty member to work on specified 
projects. The student will be required to present a number of seminars in his research area in a 
structured manner 
2. Scope of the Course 
The course broadly covers following aspects: 
(i) Research proposal 
(ii) Development related activities 
(iii) Research related activities 
The 25% weightage would be for the project proposal, which the student would be required to 
write, based on the skills acquired. For developmental activities, which carry 25%  weightage, 
the supervisor would assign to the student working with him an appropriate developmental work, 
which can be related to Centers/ Laboratories/ Assistance in course development or in the R&D 
activities of the supervisor. The student would have the teaching/research skills by assisting the 
supervisor in teaching, evaluation and research activitie s of the supervisor. Under the research 
related activities, which carries 50% weightage, a broad topic of research will be assigned to the 
higher degree student by the Supervisor and the student would conduct literature search in the 
specified area, learn various research methodologies/techniques for data collection and data 
analysis, testing techniques/methods etc. and deliver seminars in his/her research area to the 
supervisor. The student should also write research reports that along with the seminar/viva would

sources.text:
1. COURSE DESCRIPTION 
This course deals with the research and development work in assigned areas of professional 
interest. Each student will work under the overall guidance and supervision of a faculty 
member/professional. The course must end with a well defined Final Report outlining all the 
investigations, achievements and conclusions at the end of each semester. References and 
bibliography in standard format are also to be included in the report. 
 
2. SCOPE AND OBJECTIVE OF THE COURSE 
The aim of this course is to carryout a research and development project in assigned areas of 
professional interest. The course envisages student’s training in the methodology of research and 
presentation of the research findings in the form of a scientific report. 
3. OPERATION OF THE COURSE 
a) The student should immediately chalk out a plan of work in Consultation with his Supervisor. 
Current literature (journals, books, etc.) must be methodically reviewed and the status of the 
work in the field must be considered. The detailed outline of work must reflect a survey of the 
current literature in the same area and must include topic of research, objective, b ackground of 
previous work in the area, methodology and a work plan with a time schedule clearly indicating 
the intermediate milestones and the  estimated  time  to  achieve  the  same  along  with 
references and bibliography. 
b) Within two weeks of registrat ion, the student should give his Dissertation particulars to the 
Head of Department in TS-1 Performa. 
c) The student should regularly interact with his supervisor and present seminars and submit 
reports on the scheduled dates. Proposed examiners and other fac ulty in relevant area may be 
requested to attend the presentations. 
d) Supervisor will announce the Mid -semester grade to his student and send the MID -SEM 
Evaluation Form to the Head of Department. 
e) Typed copy of Final Dissertation Report and Abstract are to b e submitted to the supervisor on 
or before the last day of class work in each semester. 
f) Every student has to sign his attendance regularly with the supervisor or as per the alternative 
arrangement made by the supervisor. An attendance sheet is being provided for this purpose to 
the supervisor. 
g) The candidate should apply and seek prior permission of his supervisor for going on leave for 
any genuine needs. If leave of absence exceeds seven days in entire semester, recommended

1. Course Description: This is a course dealing with an advanced pursuit in terms of a study in assigned area 
of professional interest. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The objective of this course is to train the Ph.D. students in the art of 
research and involves various related aspects. This course helps the students in gaining deeper understanding 
of fundamental concepts and acquiring the techniques of communicating at a professional level. 
3. Operation of the course:

sources.text: Course Title             Foundations of Measurements and Experimentation
Course Title             Foundations of Measurements and Experimentation

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: This course introduces scientific and engineering inquiry through the principles 
of measurement and experimentation. It covers fundamental concepts, such as accuracy, precision, 
calibration, error analysis, and uncertainty, as well as the hands-on use of sophisticated instruments 
across multiple disciplines. The course includes data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using 
modern computational tools. It emphasizes experimental design, hypothesis formulation, and 
experimental validation. It also focuses on correlating measurements with real -world problems, 
documenting and interpreting results, and communicating findings effectively with due consideration 
to ethical practices in experimentation. 
 
2. Scope & Objective of the Course: The course aims to provide a foundational understanding of 
measurement as an essential element of engineering and scientific practice. It covers key measurement 
concepts, exposure to a variety of instruments and sensors across disciplines, and methods for reliable 
data acquisition and analysis. The objectives of the course are to enable students to: 
 
(i) Understand fundamental measurement concepts such as accuracy, precision, resolution, cali-
bration, and uncertainty. 
(ii) Use appropriate measuring instruments and sensors for acquiring experimental data across dif-
ferent domains. 
(iii)  Apply techniques for data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using modern computational 
tools. 
(iv)  Develop an understanding of experimental methodologies, including hypothesis formulation, 
experimental design, and validation. 
(v) Interpret experimental results and correlate them with underlying scientific and engineering 
principles. 
(vi)  Communicate experimental findings effectively and adhere to ethical practices in experimen-
tation and technical reporting.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:
Micro electro mechanical systems (MEMS), devices and technologies. Micro-machining and mi-
crofabrication techniques. Transduction mechanisms and modeling in different energy domains.
Analysis of micromachined capacitive, piezoresistive and thermal sensors/actuators and applica-
tions. Computer- aided design for MEMS layout, fabrication and analysis.
2. Scope & Objective of the Course:
The course introduces the basic concepts in MEMS (Micro Electromechanical Systems) with a
view to address a class of students from science and engineering disciplines. The discussion
on topics like MEMS design, Microfabrication, Microfluidics, Sensors and actuators have been
structured in the course plan. The objective of the course is to equip the students from various
aspects and with basic knowledge of the area of MEMS.

sources.text:
Makeup Policy: Makeup will be given only to genuine cases. The request application should 
reach the Instructor–in–charge before the commencement of the scheduled test. 
 
Minimum passing Marks criteria : The passing marks for this course will be determined based on 
one of the two criteria: 20% of the median of the post-comprehensive examination score OR 20% 
of the average of the first three top scorers. The lower value between these two criteria will be 
considered as passing marks in this course. NC may also be awarded if a student misses 
regular evaluation components (except lecture surprise tests) even if he/she satisfies the above 
criteria.  
 
 
IC, BITS F462/BITS U462 
Renewable energy

energy development.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Introduction to mechanics of rigid bodies and deformable bodies, Thermal 
stresses, Equilibrium of forces, Bend ing moment and shear force diagrams for determinate beams 
and frames, Analysis of statically determinate trusses; Flexural and shear Stresses in beams, 
combined stresses, Stresses and strains on inclined planes, Introduction to torsion, Torsion in 
shafts, Slope and deflection in beams due to bending, Introduction to Energy Methods, Stresses in 
thin cylindrical shells, Suspension cables, Failure theories, Buckling of columns using Euler’s Theory. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course aim s at providing overall understanding of 
various methods in understanding the behavior of structural elements under various loading 
conditions. As a part of this course, understanding of behavior of key structural materials will also 
be touched upon. Also, an overview of key structural components and their importance to 
structure will also be covered.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
Course Description: 
The compulsory disciplinary course has been designed to introduce the basic concepts of geodesy (surveying) for 
Civil Engineering students. Different basic and advanced methods of measurements and traversing have been 
included so that the student will be a ble to handle a given project independently, irrespective of whether it is a 
road or any other infrastructure project. Important issues like curve setting, calculation of areas and volumes, 
which form part and parcel of any field civil engineer in his/her day-to-day activity. Hence, in this course, these 
areas have also been included.

1. Course Description:  
Different types of cements, chemical composition, properties and tests, coarse and fine aggregate for concrete, 
tests on aggregates, grading of aggregates and its effect on concrete properties, chemical and mineral 
admixtures, properties and tests on fresh and hardened concrete; transportation and placing of concrete, non-
destructive testing of concrete, durability of concrete, quality control and acceptance criteria of concrete, 
Factors in the choice of mix proportions, Proportioning of concrete mixes by various methods – BIS method 
of mix design; Introduction to special concretes. Manufacturing/sources, classification, applications, 
properties and testing of bricks, blocks, tiles, aggregates,  lime, timber, paints, glass, bitumen, cutback, 
emulsion, modified bitumen, steel, non-ferrous metals, polymeric materials, geo-synthetics, etc. Low cost and 
waste material in construction. Latest, BIS, IRC & ASTM specifications and guidelines of all above-
mentioned material, and construction equipment.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Fluid Mechanics is an introductory course that covers the fundamental aspects of fluid mechanics, 
especially the classical and well -established laws. This course emphasizes understanding these governing 
laws and their widespread engineering applications in fluid related problems by covering the following 
topics: Concepts and defin itions, compressibility of fluids, fluid pressure and measurement, fluid statics, 
buoyancy, rigid body motion, fluid kinematics, conservation laws: control volume approach, differential 
analysis of fluid flow, study of flow pattern through orifices and mouthpieces, notches and weirs, analysis 
of flow through pipes, viscous fluid flow analysis: analysis of flow through pipes, dimensional analysis and 
similitude. 
The contents of this course will enable the students to tackle real-life fluid mechanics problems and provide 
a broad overview of the subject. Moreover, this course will be helpful to students as a prerequisite for further 
advanced courses in fluid mechanics at undergraduate and graduate levels. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
• Introduction to different fluid properties and their engineering applications 
• Learn about pressure exerted by fluids and pressure measurement techniques 
• Estimate hydrostatic forces on surfaces 
• Learn about buoyancy and evaluate stability of submerged and floating bodies 
• Understand concepts of fluid kinematics, methods of describing fluid flow, types of fluid flow, 
control mass and control volume, rate of flow, continuity equation, potential and stream functions 
• Study dynamics of fluid flow, Euler’s equation, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications, Navier 
Stokes equation, and pipe bend problems 
• Compute fluid discharge through orifices and mouthpieces, and flow over weirs and notches 
• Analyze flow of viscous fluids through pipes and plates, and compute head loss due to friction 
• Compute different types of energy losses and determine hydraulic gradient and total energy line for 
flow through pipes. Become adept at solving problems pertaining to syphon, flow through pipes in 
series, parallel and branched pipes, power transmission through pipes, and flow through nozzles 
• Perceive the concepts of dimensional analysis and similitude

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
This course introduces Civil Engineering students to the core concepts of hydraulic engineering, focusing 
on the Behaviour of real fluids: boundary layer theory, turbulent flow through conduits; analysis of 
closed-conduit hydraulic systems including pipes, valves, fittings, and pumps, water hammer in 
pipes, pipe networks analysis: Hardy cross method; Open channel hydraulics: uniform and non -
uniform flow; flow past immersed bodies: drag and lift; Analysis of Impact of jets; Introduction to 
fluid machinery. 
2. Scope & Course Objective: 
The problems encountered by our society, such as water supply, irrigation, navigation, and water power, 
resulted in the development of Fluid Mechanics and Hydraulic Engineering. The objective of this course is 
to equip students with a fundamental understanding of the principles of fluid mechanics as applied to 
hydraulic systems and structures. The course aims to achieve the following  Course Objectives (Teacher's 
perspective), aligned with the Course Outcomes (COs) (Students’ perspective): 
1. To develop an analytical understanding of flow behavior in pipes and channels under varying conditions. 
2. To apply fluid mechanics principles in analyzing hydraulic systems, including energy losses and force 
impacts. 
3. To introduce the working principles and performance of fluid machinery relevant to civil engineering. 
4. To prepare students for practical problem -solving in the analysis, design, and assessment of water 
infrastructures of Pipe networks, open channels, and structures submerged in fluid, like bridge piers,  
dealt with by civil engineers. 
 
3. Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs):

1. Course Description: General requirement for satisfactory performance of shallow foundations, general, local and punching 
shear failures, bearing capacity, settlement, tilt and rotation of foundations, proportioning of Shallow Foundations, footings on 
layered soils and slopes, Deep foundations, capacity of single and group Piles, laterally loaded pile, Earth Pressure  theories, 
Retaining structures, design and checks for stability, Stability of slopes, Introduction to Ground Improvement Techniques and  
geosynthetics with applications, Introduction to machine foundations for different type of machines, Introduction to ge otechnical 
earthquake engineering and liquefaction of soils, computer applications in foundation  design 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The main goal of this course is to provide an in -depth understanding regarding 
different types of foundations. An alysis of foundations and retaining structures (Shallow foundations, pile foundations, machine 
foundations, retaining walls, slope stability etc.) considering all geotechnical aspects. Emphasis will be given on complete coverage 
of code of practices for various types of foundations and retaining structures. Geotechnical earthquake engineering, ground 
improvement techniques, reinforced earth walls and geosynthetics applications increased tremendously therefore given due 
consideration.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Design Philosophies: Introduction to working stress design philosophy; Limit State design philosophy, 
Limit State design of Singly reinforced and doubly reinforced rectangular and flanged section beams; 
Design of one-way and two-way slabs in flexure; Design of beams and slabs for shear; Design of beams 
and slabs for bond, anchorage and development length;  Design of beams and slabs for  serviceability ; 
Limit state design of columns subjected to axial load, and axial load plus uni-axial and  bi-axial bending; 
Design of footings under the columns; Design of simple staircases. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course 
In this course, the students will be introduced to the various design philosophies used in the design of 
Reinforced Concrete (RC) structures, with a particular focus on the Limit State Design method. The 
course will provide an in-depth discussion of the concepts of Limit State Design method. Subsequently, 
the Limit State Design method will be employed to the design of singly and doubly reinforced 
rectangular- and T-section beams and one-way and two-way slabs, for flexure, shear, anchorage, bond, 
and serviceability requirement. Additionally, the course will cover the design of columns subjected to 
axial loads, and axial load plus uniaxial and biaxial moments. Moreover, the course will explore different 
types of staircases, with a specific emphasis on the design of dog -legged staircases.  At the end of this 
course, students will be able to design the basic structural elements of an RC buildings.

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
Course description: In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering is an introductory course to 
various in -situ test methods pertaining to geotechnical engineering and analysis of in -situ test results, 
including drilling and sampling, standard penetration test (SPT), con e-penetration test (CPT), piezocone 
penetration test (CPTu), vane shear test (VST), non-destructive tests (NDT) using body waves and surface 
waves - seismic reflection test, seismic refraction test, and spectral analysis of surface waves (SASW) test. 
Structure and components of geotechnical reports and data presentation techniques using borehole logs will 
be discussed. The contents of this course will enable students to utilize different in-situ test results for soil 
property interpretation, direct and indirect applications for the design of geotechnical structures, and 
liquefaction assessment. This course will be helpfu l to students when they start working as practicing 
engineers or for further graduate-level advanced courses in geotechnical engineering.

Course Title :  Fundamentals of Systems Engineering

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: Systems Engineering is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on 
the structured development, integration, and management of complex systems 
across their entire life cycle —from conceptual design and planning to operation, 
maintenance, and retirement. In the context of infrastructure, it addresses technical, 
organizational, a nd stakeholder -related complexities by employing a holistic, 
systems-oriented approach. This course introduces students to the fundamentals of 
systems engineering with a focus on civil and infrastructure systems, preparing them 
to think critically and act strategically in dynamic, real-world environments.

sources.text: Course Title : Transportation Systems Planning and Management
Course Title : Transportation Systems Planning and Management

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: System and environment; sequential transportation systems planning: 
trip generation, trip distribution, modal split and traffic assignment, Transportation surveys, 
Land-use models, Travel demand forecasting, Urban structure and its influence of travel 
intensity, Urban goods movement. Transportation Systems Management (TSM) actions: traffic 
management techniques for improving vehicular flow, preferential treatment for high 
occupancy modes, demand management technique for reduced traffic demand, staggered hours, 
vehicle restrictions; planning for pedestrians. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The course aims at imparting knowledge on 
understanding of urban transportation problems in planners’ perspective, definition of the 
problem, setting clear goals and objectives to serve as guiding factors in the planning process, 
identification of the causal factors influencing the demand for urban travel and development of 
relationship between the factors and the travel demand.

the primary focus will be on building

sources.text:
Instructor-in-charge : ANSHUMAN 
Room No.                      : 1232 (FD-I) 12 Noon – 12.50 PM 
 
1 Course Description: The course deals with planning techniques, engineering economy, valuation including 
estimation & costing, system design, construction methodologies ranging from small buildings to large 
infrastructure projects, construction technologies including recent ad vancements. Relevant Indian Standard 
codes of practices will be given emphasis. 
 
2 (a): Scope of the Course: 
The scope of the course is to know the various aspects of construction planning and management right from 
the knowledge of various activities till the estimation, costing, valuation, tendering etc., Though this course 
covers wider infrastructure projects, the primary focus will be on building and road infrastructure.  
 
2(b): Objectives of the course: 
 
➢ To understand the different construction projects and basic objective of project management [Module 
- I] 
➢ To understand the project management techniques (CPM and PERT) [Module - II] 
➢ To analyze the various requirements of manpower and other resources [ Module-III] 
➢ To analyze the various control methodologies keeping in line with project requirements [Module-IV] 
➢ To get exposed to construction contracts and tenders [Module-V] 
➢ To estimate the quantity and rate of different building components (including materials) [Module VI] 
➢ To discuss the various aspects of valuation of properties [Module VII] 
➢ To highlights various aspects of construction quality and safety with case studies [Module VIII] 
➢ To understand the best practices of construction management [Module IX]

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: [as per the Bulletin]  
This course covers topics related to characterization of pavement materials including soil, 
aggregates, bitumen,bituminous mixtures and pavement quality concrete (PQC). Soil 
characterization includes description of characteristics and desirable properties,  classification, 
compaction, strength and modulus of subgrade soil. For aggregates, origin and production, 
mineralogy, physical properties and aggregate properties for mix design would be discussed. 
Detailed description of bituminous binder would include o rigin, production and it application, 
chemical composition, physical and rheological properties, grading system, modification of 
bitumen, cutbacks and emulsions. Bituminous mixtures include production, desirable properties, 
mix design and performance testing. For PQC, materials and selection of mix proportions would 
be covered along with design example.

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: [as per the Bulletin]  
This course covers topics related to characterization of pavement materials including soil, 
aggregates, bitumen,bituminous mixtures and pavement quality concrete (PQC). Soil 
characterization includes description of characteristics and desirable properties,  classification, 
compaction, strength and modulus of subgrade soil. For aggregates, origin and production, 
mineralogy, physical properties and aggregate properties for mix design would be discussed. 
Detailed description of bituminous binder would include o rigin, production and it application, 
chemical composition, physical and rheological properties, grading system, modification of 
bitumen, cutbacks and emulsions. Bituminous mixtures include production, desirable properties, 
mix design and performance testing. For PQC, materials and selection of mix proportions would 
be covered along with design example.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: The course deals with complete planning and design of airports with greater emphasis 
on planning not restricted to airports, but air transport at large. The course will also touch base on several other 
connected aspects of air transportation such as forecasting air transport demand, evolution of aircraft and 
pavements, air transportation business, sustainability aspects etc., 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The scope of the course is to know  the various aspects of airport 
planning and design. This course is expected to provide a broad overview on various topics as mentioned 
below. 
 
➢ To understand briefly air transport and aviation industry [Module I] 
➢ To understand the need to forecast air transport demand [Module II] 
➢ To get the overall idea about aircraft and its influence on entire planning [Module III] 
➢ To get a comprehensive overview about airport system and master planning [Module IV] 
➢ To get an overview about the factors affecting the airport capacity [Module V] 
➢ To comprehensively analyze the airside configuration and geometric design [Module VI] 
➢ To understand the structural pavement design and airport drainage [Module VII] 
➢ To get a quick overview about different visual aids in airport and in airspace [Module VIII] 
➢ To acknowledge the importance of maintenance and rehabilitation of pavement [Module IX] 
➢ To know the parameters influencing the airport performance including benchmarking [Module X]
