syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Destructive testing: Tensile testing: Elastic modulus – Applications of elastic 
deformation - Case studies in modulus limited design; Strength and ductility – Case studies in yield 
limited design; Fracture – Case studies in fracture; Fatigue and Creep tests – Case studies in fatigue 
and creep failure. Corrosion tests – Types of corrosion – Case studies in wet corrosion. Non -
destructive testing: Overview of the non -destructive testing; detection of surface flaws, detection of 
internal flaws, and Case studies . Materials selection in mechanical design - Materials properties 
charts – Basics of materials selection – Minimum mass design – Deflection limited design; Material 
selection for flywheels, springs, coupling, shaker tables and pressure vessels. Designing h ybrid 
materials – Composites – Sandwich structures – Lattice structures.AI tools for materials selection.  
Lab: • Quasi -static and high -strain-rate testing of materials to determine their elastic and plastic 
properties.• Fatigue and Creep tests to determine the dynamic properties of materials • Experiments 
to determine the corrosion rate • non -destructive tests  by DPT, MPI and Ultrasonic studies • 
Simulation studies on materials selection using ANSYS Granta Selector. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
 
3. Text Book(s) 
T1 William D Calister Jr,” Material Science & Engineering, an Introduction”, John Wiley & Sons, 
New York. 8th edition 
T2 George E. Dieter, ‘Mechanical Metallurgy’, McGraw Hill, SI Metric Edition 
 
Reference Book(s) & other resources 
R1 William F. Smith, Javad Hashemi, ‘Material Science& Engineering”, In SI unitsFourth 
edition, McGraw-Hill.

Butterworth-Heinemann publisher

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1.  Course Description:  
Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel 
operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion; 
Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations, 
classification. D.C generators, per formance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed 
control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic 
field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time 
harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase ind uction motors - classification and 
equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors; 
equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation. 
Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and 
speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.    
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt 
power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating character istics of 
Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this 
course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical -magnetic devices such as Transformer, 
DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed exper imental component for better 
understanding of the concepts.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
Course Description: 
Analysis and design of communication systems; analog and digital modulation and demodulation, frequency 
conversion, multiplexing, noise and distortion; spectral and signal-to-noise ratio analysis, probability of error in digital 
systems, spread spectrum.Introduction to the basic principles of the design and analysis of modern digital 
communication systems. Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation 
techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization 
 
1. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication 
system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block 
diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which 
are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital 
communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. 
 
The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of 
random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR 
and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon 
theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication 
systems using MATLAB and Python software. 
 
The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog 
and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced 
level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on 
communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of 
Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
Course Description:  
Review of Maxwell's equations; Wave propagation: Normal & Oblique incidence; Transmission 
Lines & Smith Chart, Waveguide: Rectangular & Cylindrical waveguides; Dielectric 
Waveguides; Cavity resonato r, equivalent Circuit Model, characteristics; Microwave devices 
(Waveguide based and planar); S parameters; Measurement & Impedance Matching; M icrowave 
Generators & Amplifiers; Antennas and its characteristics and types. 
Scope and objective of the course:  
This course provides a comprehensive understanding of electromagnetic wave theory and 
microwave engineering, focusing on Maxwell’s equations, wave propagation, and transmission 
line theory. It covers the analysis and design of waveguides, cavity resonator s, and dielectric 
structures. Students will explore microwave devices, S -parameters, impedance matching 
techniques, and measurement methods. The course also introduces microwave generators, 
amplifiers, and various types of antennas with their characteristi cs. The objective is to equip 
students with the theoretical foundation and practical skills needed to analyze, design, and apply 
high-frequency systems in modern communication, radar, and sensing applications.

List of Experiments  
Simulation based on CST 
1. Design and analysis of microstrip lines (probably 1 – 3 labs): 
a. Varying width (W) and substrates (εr)  plot Zo vs W for different εr (at least 10 points) 
b. Design load terminations: matched/unmatched with those of the microstrip line’s 
characteristic impedance  port and discrete impedance  
c. Design of a quarter-wave transformer matching network for single, double, triple stages, 
plot Γ vs f 
d. Design a λ/2 line and analyze the input impedance  
2. Design of matching networks: (2 labs) 
a. Design of FDCL (frequency-dependent complex loads) at 2.45, 5.8 GHz: Emulation of 
inductive and capacitive loads with the TX line  
b. Design of an impedance matching network with series/shunt stub 
3. Design of planar microwave devices: (2 labs) 
a. Waveguides 
b. E- and H-plane Tees 
c. Coupler and attenuator (if possible)  
4. Introduction to antenna design: (2 labs)  
a. Design of dipole and monopole patch antennas  
b. Design different feeding mechanisms  
c. Introduction to FSS

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
Introduction; design of analog filters; design of digital filters (IIR and FIR); structures for the realization of 
digital filters; random signals and random processes; li near estimation and prediction; Wiener filters; DSP 
processor architecture; DSP algorithms for different applications. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  
 
a) To provide a comprehensive knowledge of DSP's fundamental theory, concepts, and applications.  
b) To be able to design and simulate practical DSP-based systems, finding applications in various fields, 
namely, communication engineering, audio, video, and image signal processing.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description 
This course is a foundation course for the students entering into the discipline of Economics & Finance. 
This introductory course teaches the basic concepts related to the economic system that are listed as 
follows: Introduction to Economics (Microeconomics) & Economic Problems; Demand, Supply, & 
Elasticity; Household Behavior and Consumer choice; The Production Process; Costs and Output 
Decisions; Demand for Production Inputs; Market Imperfections: Monopoly, Oligopoly, Monopolistic 
Competition; Introduction to Macroeconomics and the Problems; Measurement of National Income & 
Output; Money Supply and the Banking System 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course 
The main objective is to introduce the fundamental concepts and tools necessary to acquire an 
understanding of economic decision making of market participants such as Individual households, firms, 
and the government. The course covers two major areas of economics namely Microeconomics and 
Macroeconomics. The knowledge of the fundamentals would help the students to better understand the 
entire economic system and the process followed in policy making. This course would lay foundation 
for the students to understand other related courses in economics & finance such as Mathematical 
Economics, International Economics, Advance Micro and Macroeconomics, among others.

sources.text: Course Title : [Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting]
Course Title : [Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting]

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: 
 Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not  
only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also  
communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize  
transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails 
two important and interrelated aspects, i.e., 
a. Recording transactions, and 
b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc. 
Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing 
financial statements. 
The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules  
of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial 
balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership,  
credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the  
statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold,  
recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets. 
This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students 
and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from 
Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and  
financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced  
courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent  
semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance.  
Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the  
field of finance.

COURSE TITLE : MATHEMATICAL AND STATISTICAL METHODS

syllabus.heading: COURSE DESCRIPTION

sources.text:
1. COURSE DESCRIPTION 
The course is designed to provide a basic understanding of various statistical and mathematical methods useful for 
decision-making and for understanding applications in other economics and finance courses. The course is divided into 
two part s: Statistical Methods and Mathematical Methods. Statistical Methods include methods of collecting and 
describing statistical data – types of data and data collection methodologies, sampling methods & design, data 
describing methods (graphical and numerical); Correlation and Regre ssion analyses; Index numbers: Concepts, uses, 
and methods of construction; Analysis of Time-series: Components, data generating process, and stationarity; Statistical 
Inference: Introduction to  Probability and its distributions , sampling distributions, theory of estimation , Tests of 
Hypotheses testing (Parametric & Non -Parametric); and Mathematical Methods  include Concepts from Linear 
Algebra & their Applications  (Matrices, Input-Output analysis, and Game Theory ); Concepts from Calculus and their 
applications; Introduction to Optimization in Economics and its Applications.

sources.text: Course Title                : ECONOMIC ENVIRONMENT OF BUSINESS
Course Title                : ECONOMIC ENVIRONMENT OF BUSINESS

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
Businesses are the driving force behind a nation's economic activity since they enable its 
population to attain a higher quality of living. It is essential to understand that a business firm does 
not operate in a vacuum but in a given environment and must interact and transact its business 
within this environment. Business environment refers to the totality of all individuals, institutions, 
and other forces external to a business unit but potentially affecting  its performance. Business 
enterprises are micro units within an economic environment that represents the macro. The 
economic environment is the “given” within which firms and their managements must operate. So, 
the business environment and the manner and effectiveness of the interaction of an enterprise with 
its environment would generally determine its success or failure.  
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
The course aims to (1) Create familiarity with economic environment concepts and indicators, 
economic policies , and economic regulation (2) Develop the ability to analyze and anticipate 
changes in the economic environment and, (3) Enable students to take more effective business 
decisions by being responsive to the changing external economic environment.  The objective of 
this course is to unravel all those economic factors that are external to and beyond the  control of 
individual business enterprises and their management, with a focus on the Indian context.  
 
3. Learning Outcome of the Course: 
This course will educate students on the interdependencies and linkages between business and its 
environment, focusing on the Indian context. Moreover, it will improve comprehension of various 
external economic factors affecting the business environment. For instance, the business climate 
in India is influenced by variables such as GDP, inflation, fiscal policy, monetary policy, industrial 
policy, etc., which have both direct and indirect effects. Furthermore, it will thoroughly 
comprehend many economic elements in the business environment more pragmatically. 
4. Textbooks and Reference Books 
4.1 Text Books (TB): 
TB1. Pailwar, Veena Keshav., “Business Environment”, PHI Learning Private Limited 
(2014).

not operate in a vacuum but in a given environment and must interact and transact its business 
within this environment. Business environment refers to the totality of all individuals, institutions, 
and other forces external to a business unit but potentially affecting  its performance. Business 
enterprises are micro units within an economic environment that represents the macro. The 
economic environment is the “given” within which firms and their managements must operate. So, 
the business environment and the manner and effectiveness of the interaction of an enterprise with 
its environment would generally determine its success or failure.  
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
The course aims to (1) Create familiarity with economic environment concepts and indicators, 
economic policies , and economic regulation (2) Develop the ability to analyze and anticipate 
changes in the economic environment and, (3) Enable students to take more effective business 
decisions by being responsive to the changing external economic environment.  The objective of 
this course is to unravel all those economic factors that are external to and beyond the  control of 
individual business enterprises and their management, with a focus on the Indian context.  
 
3. Learning Outcome of the Course: 
This course will educate students on the interdependencies and linkages between business and its 
environment, focusing on the Indian context. Moreover, it will improve comprehension of various 
external economic factors affecting the business environment. For instance, the business climate 
in India is influenced by variables such as GDP, inflation, fiscal policy, monetary policy, industrial 
policy, etc., which have both direct and indirect effects. Furthermore, it will thoroughly 
comprehend many economic elements in the business environment more pragmatically. 
4. Textbooks and Reference Books 
4.1 Text Books (TB): 
TB1. Pailwar, Veena Keshav., “Business Environment”, PHI Learning Private Limited 
(2014).

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description 
This course develops a systematic exposition of both classical and modern theories of international trade in 
goods and services that try to explain the composition, direction, and consequences of international trade, and 
the determinants and effects of trade policy. The course will look critically at the welfare and profit 
implications of trade policy deviations from free trade. It then builds on the models of open economy 
macroeconomics. 
 
2. Scope and objective of the course: 
 To understand the effects of international trade on individuals and businesses  
 To understand the effects of changes in trade policies on trade  
 To apply macroeconomic models to understand the international economy.  
 To focus on the interrelationships among aggregate economic variables such as GDP, 
unemployment rates, inflation rates, trade balances, exchange rates, interest rates, etc.  
 To focus on the significance of trade imbalances, the determinants of exchange rates, and the 
aggregate effects of government monetary and fiscal policies.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Money and its functions; money market; foreign exchange market; financial market; financial derivatives; the 
banking firm; non-banking financial institutions; Indian banking; monetary transmission mechanisms; money 
and inflation; central banking; determinants of money supply; tools, goals and targets of monetary policy; 
international monetary and financial system. 
2. Scope & Objective of the Course: 
 To study the mechanisms of debt market and role played by interest rate 
 To study the dynamics and money market and stock market 
 To explore the structure of financial system and understand the reasons financial crisis 
 To understand the role of central banks and commercial banks in regulation money supply in the economy. 
 To discuss the role of central banks in the conduct of monetary policy 
 To study the foreign exchange rate dynamics and foreign exchange risk 
 To discuss the risk management techniques for financial institutions.

This course provides a comprehensive and contemporary examination of the major issues, challenges, and policy 
debates in economic development by integrating theoretical perspectives, empirical evidence, and real -world 
applications. It views development as a multidimensional process that extends beyond economic growth to encompass 
structural transformation, human development, institutional quality, technological progress, environmental 
sustainability, and social inclusion. The course explores why countries exper ience divergent development trajectories 
and examines the roles of markets, governments, institutions, globalization, and technological change in shaping long-
run development outcomes. Drawing upon classical and contemporary development theories, with particular emphasis 
on India and other de veloping economies, the course examines a broad range of development issues, including 
poverty, inequality, unemployment, population dynamics, demographic transition, migration, urbanization, education, 
health, agriculture, industrialization, infrastructure, financial inclusion, foreign investment, governance, environmental 
degradation, climate change, artificial intelligence and development , digital transformation, and the Sustainable 
Development Goals (SDGs). Through a nalytical frameworks, empirical evidence, policy debates, and case studies, 
students will develop the ability to critically examine development challenges, interpret development indicators, and 
evaluate alternative policy interventions for achieving sustainable, inclusive, and equitable development.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as 
a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial 
decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate 
level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic 
experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of 
Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by 
the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm. 
In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements, 
the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of 
firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other 
are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available 
to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with 
uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of 
fault lines in the financial markets. 
To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress 
suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More 
importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C -suite 
managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm 
must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment, 
investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing 
policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy. 
The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital, 
investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and 
sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
This course focuses on the essential tools and frameworks for evaluating the value of companies through 
financial analysis. Students will explore key concepts such as internal growth, mergers and acquisitions, along 
with valuation methodologies like discounted cash flow and relative valuation. Designed for those with prior 
knowledge in finance and accounting, the course equips students with the skills to analyze financial statements, 
assess market conditions, and identify key performance drivers. Ideal for aspiring professionals in investment 
banking, corporate finance, and consulting, this course enhances analytical capabilities and strategic thinking 
in business valuation and decision-making. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
The Process of measuring and managing the value of companies is a central aspect of financial analysis. 
Globally, managers are in pursuit of adding value to their firms via two important means. One, by enhancing 
the firm’s productive capacity through internal (or organic) growth, which has a simultaneous positive 
impact on its stock price. Second, through mergers and acquisitions (a decision involving factors external 
to the firm) that int erlocks with corporation’s key strengths, and yield benefits in the long run. Hence, 
asking, “What is something worth?” is a  vital question to business decision making, and the principal 
objective behind this course is to provide the learners with the conceptual basis, intuitive reasoning, and 
analytical framework to answer this question. 
The focus of this course is on valuing equity (or ownership) in a firm and estimating the value of the overall 
enterprise. The coverage relies on discounted cash flow, rela tive valuation, and contingent valuation 
approaches for extracting the value of a business. Since financial statements serve as the basis for all types 
of valuation methods, the course begins by providing brief framework on the principles governing the 
financial statements, and adjustments that are often required to capture the underlying business reality. 
Students who are either currently pursuing or would like to embark on a career in investment banking, 
corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting will find the course material to 
be most useful. The course also carries a broader appeal to individuals who are interested in enhancing 
their understanding of financial analysis, and in learning how businesses measure and create value for their 
investors.

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected 
problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold. 
The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return 
profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental, 
quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy, 
industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation 
forms a major component of this course. 
Another important aspect of the course is on modern portfolio concepts, where the criterion changes: 
a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the 
whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the 
construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
The Financial Engineering Concentration encompasses the design, analysis, and construction of financial 
contracts to meet the needs of enterprises. It involves developing and creatively applying financial theory and 
financial instruments to structure solutions to complex financial problems and exploit financial opportunities.   
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
The objective of the course is to provide a preliminary understanding of financial engineering tools and 
techniques in the present market environment, such as applications of futures and options for hedging, asset 
price dynamics, and the use of simulation in decision-making. Financial Engineering is a multidisciplinary 
field involving financial theory, the methods of engineering, the tools of mathematics, and the practice of 
programming. The course on financial engineering would enable students to respond to the professional 
requirements particularly related to investment banking, financial management, treasury operations, asset 
management, risk management, consulting and capital markets, etc.

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are 
expected to create a technology product -based or s ervice/SaaS-based startup and complete the business 
model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture.  
In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases 
of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3) 
go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations  and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on 
customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive 
analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guest-
lectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running 
Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide 
them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded.  The top teams may be 
invited to compete for  seed funding in early 202 7 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the 
completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business.  
2. Scope & Objective of the Course:  
NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence, 
the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC 
helps them to think and act entrepreneurially.  The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform 
an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a 
reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific 
market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build 
an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win 
customers? How wil l your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key 
external partners?

Tutorial/Practical Instructors : -- 
1 Course Description: 
Introduction to risk; types of risk; risk measurement; risk management techniques; risk avoidance, loss control, loss financing, risk retenti on, 
risk transfer, internal risk reduction through diversification etc.; insurance business and operations; insurance pricing; insurance v/s hedging; 
life, health and income risk; property and liability risk – commercial and personal; social insurance; insurance regulation 
2 Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This course will examine the way in which business and society make an assessment of, control and transfer risk. The scope of  this course 
is to provide a broad understanding of risk and insurance as a means to manage it. This forms the foundation to facilitate the students in their 
further studies on insurance. The course introduces the concept of risk and techniques of identifying, measuring and managing  it. In this 
context, insurance as a risk management tool is discussed with references to its role, functions and basic principles as applicable to different 
classes of insurance.  
The objectives of the course are to provide students with 
 a comprehensive understanding for making risk management decisions to increase business value and individual welfare  
 a complete understanding of risk transfer through pooling and key features of insurance market  
 an understanding of the effects of and rationale for public policies that affect risk and its allocation  
 Knowledge about insurance markets and important details of an insurance contract as a risk management tool. 
 Assessing and evaluating insurance needs and implement effective solutions, involving and aligning the entire organization 
3 Text Book: 
George Rejda and Michael McNamara ‘Principles of Risk Management and Insurance’ 14th edition, Pearson Education, 2022 (ISBN 
9780134082578)

Course Title              : Environmental Sampling and Analytical Methods

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Principles of sample collection and data analysis/interpretation, Gravimetric methods, 
titrimetric methods, electrochemical methods, Spectrometric method of analysis, Chromatographic method of 
analysis, sampling techniques for air and water pollution, Biological methods of analysis, Interpretatio n of 
data in environmental monitoring. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  The course introduces methodology of sample collection (sampling 
techniques) for water/wastewater/air . The course covers various aspects of sample analysis through 
conventional ( for example gravimetric, titrimetric) and advanced methods ( for example electrochemical, 
spectrophotometric, chromatographic ). The course will also guide students, to apply concepts for 
environmental monitoring.

sources.text:
1. Course description: Urban Water Management is an advanced course focusing on the 
planning, design, operation, and assessment of urban water systems under increasing 
pressures of population growth, urbanization, and climate change. It explores the 
complete urban water cycle, i ncluding supply, sanitation, drainage, and 
environmental flows, with strong emphasis on sustainable and resilient urban 
development. The course addresses technical, social, economic, and regulatory 
challenges through a multidisciplinary lens. Students are exposed to contemporary 
topics such as stormwater management, water -sensitive urban design, and water 
quality monitoring. Practical software -based training modules on stormwater 
modelling, flood forecasting, and hydroinformatics are integrated to bridge th eory 
and real -world applications. Students will also gain insights into advanced asset 
management systems, sustainability indicators, GIS tools, and the effect of 
urbanization on hydrological behavior. This industry -oriented course prepares 
students for pr ofessional roles in government, consulting, and research sectors 
concerned with smart, equitable, and sustainable urban water solutions.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1.  Course Description:  
Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel 
operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion; 
Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations, 
classification. D.C generators, per formance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed 
control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic 
field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time 
harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase ind uction motors - classification and 
equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors; 
equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation. 
Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and 
speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.    
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt 
power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating character istics of 
Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this 
course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical -magnetic devices such as Transformer, 
DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed exper imental component for better 
understanding of the concepts.

Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations, 
classification. D.C generators, per formance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed 
control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic 
field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time 
harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase ind uction motors - classification and 
equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors; 
equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation. 
Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and 
speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.    
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt 
power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating character istics of 
Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this 
course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical -magnetic devices such as Transformer, 
DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed exper imental component for better 
understanding of the concepts.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Basic microelectronic circuit analysis and design, biasing in discrete and integrated 
circuit amplifiers, an overview of modeling of microelectronic devices single and two transistor amplifier 
configurations with passive and active loads; current mirrors & current sources; single-ended and differential 
linear amplifiers , differential and multistage amplifiers; 2 stage CMOS OPAMP, frequency response of 
amplifiers; negative feedback in amplifiers, R-C frequency compensation. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
The objective of this course is to develop the ability to analyze and design integrated electronic 
circuits. The course aims to provide a thorough understanding of electronic circuits & building blocks 
necessary for the effective realization of analog integrated circuits. The course also includes the usage 
of SPICE as a circuit design aid.  
3. Learning outcomes of the Course: 
 Understand device modelling, two-port network models, and amplifier characterization parameters   
 Understand the necessity of and techniques to set DC bias, Quiescent point location for different types 
of amplifiers.  
 Understand analysis and synthesis of different single/ multi -stage amplifiers  and their 
characterization. 
 Design of amplifiers using EDA tools.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
Course Description: 
Analysis and design of communication systems; analog and digital modulation and demodulation, frequency 
conversion, multiplexing, noise and distortion; spectral and signal-to-noise ratio analysis, probability of error in digital 
systems, spread spectrum.Introduction to the basic principles of the design and analysis of modern digital 
communication systems. Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation 
techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization 
 
1. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication 
system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block 
diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which 
are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital 
communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. 
 
The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of 
random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR 
and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon 
theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication 
systems using MATLAB and Python software. 
 
The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog 
and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced 
level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on 
communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of 
Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.

4. Course Plan: 
 
Module No. Lecture Session Reference Learning Objectives 
 
 
(I): 
Introduction to 
Communication 
Systems and 
Bandwidth (2 
Lectures) 
Lectures 1–2: Overview of the course; 
taxonomy of communication systems; block-
level description of an end-to-end 
communication system; baseband and 
passband transmission; brief review of the 
Fourier transform and signal spectrum; signal 
bandwidth, channel bandwidth and 
bandwidth requirements in communication 
systems. 
T1: chapters 1, 2  Describe the functional 
blocks of an end-to-end 
communication system; 
distinguish between 
baseband and passband 
transmission; interpret 
communication signals in the 
time and frequency domains; 
and relate signal bandwidth 
to channel bandwidth. 
 
 
 
(II): 
Analog modulation 
and Demodulation (12 
Lectures) 
Lectures 3–10:  Amplitude-modulation 
techniques: DSB-SC, AM with carrier, SSB-SC, 
VSB; angle-modulation techniques: 
frequency modulation and phase 
modulation; bandwidth and power 
requirements; generation of AM and FM 
signals; Armstrong method of FM generation; 
and frequency-division multiplexing. 
T1: chapters 3,4 
 
Explain frequency translation 
and the principles of 
amplitude and angle 
modulation; compare analog 
modulation schemes in terms 
of bandwidth and power 
requirements; describe 
methods for generating AM, 
FM and PM signals; and 
explain frequency-division 
multiplexing. 
Lectures 11–14:  Synchronous detection; 
envelope detection; FM and PM 
demodulation; phase-locked-loop- based 
demodulation; and superheterodyne 
receivers. 
T1: chapter 3,4 
 
Explain synchronous and 
envelope detection; describe 
FM- and PM-demodulation 
techniques, including PLL-
based demodulation; and 
explain the architecture and 
operation of a 
superheterodyne receiver. 
 
 
 
(III) 
Communication 
Channels and Noise 
(10 Lectures)  
Lectures  15-19: Communication media and 
channel models; signal transmission over 
communication channels; conditions for 
distortionless transmission; amplitude and phase 
distortion; random variables and random 
processes; statistical averages; autocorrelation 
and power spectral density; Gaussian processes; 
bandpass random processes; sources and nature 
of noise; additive white Gaussian noise; and noise 
figure. 
T1: chapter 
2,6,7 
 
Explain communication-media 
and channel models; identify 
amplitude and phase 
distortion; apply random-
variable and random-process 
concepts in communication-
system analysis; interpret 
autocorrelation and power 
spectral density; and explain 
Gaussian noise, bandpass 
noise, AWGN and noise 
figure.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
Course Description: 
Analysis and design of communication systems; analog and digital modulation and demodulation, frequency 
conversion, multiplexing, noise and distortion; spectral and signal-to-noise ratio analysis, probability of error in digital 
systems, spread spectrum.Introduction to the basic principles of the design and analysis of modern digital 
communication systems. Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation 
techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization 
 
1. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication 
system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block 
diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which 
are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital 
communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. 
 
The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of 
random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR 
and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon 
theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication 
systems using MATLAB and Python software. 
 
The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog 
and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced 
level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on 
communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of 
Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
 
This course introduces students to the principles and practical aspects of designing integrated circuits using 
CMOS technology. It covers both analog and digital VLSI design methodologies, exploring circuit -level 
building blocks, layout considerations, and performance trade-offs. Emphasis is placed on low-power, area-
efficient, and high -performance circuit techniques, along with exp osure to modern CAD tools and 
fabrication-aware design strategies. Students will gain experience designing critical components, including 
logic gates, adders, amplifiers, and mixed-signal interfaces.

Course Title                    : FPGA BASED SYSTEM DESIGN

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1.   Course Description: 
Digital system design options and t rade-offs, design methodology and technology overview,  
Programmable Logic Devices, SPLDs, CPLDs, and Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs); FPGA 
architectural options, granularity of function and wiring resources, coarse vs. fine -grained, vendor-specific 
issues (emphasis on Xilinx and Altera), Logic fabric, Look -up tables, block BRAMs, DSP slices etc., 
timing models, power dissipation, Input and Output cell characteristics, clock input, Timing, Power 
dissipation, Programmable interconnect, Hardware Descrip tion Languages, FPGA system design tools, 
synthesis, and implementation, design verification and debugging, FPGA based design studies, interfacing 
with input-output devices and data converters. 
 
2.   Scope and Objective of the Course:  
This course aims to upskill the students with the following topics: 
 Build a strong foundation in FPGA architecture, technologies, and design methodologies. 
 Develop proficiency in HDL-based design for creating complex digital systems. 
 Explore the full FPGA design flow—from concept to implementation and debugging. 
 Integrate embedded processors, IP cores, and DSP functions into FPGA-based designs. 
 Apply knowledge through hands-on labs and projects using modern FPGA platforms. 
 
3. Course Learning O utcomes: Students will gain a com prehensive understanding of FPGA 
architecture and design flow, develop proficiency in HDL -based digital design, and learn to integrat e 
digital s ystem, embedded processors, and IP cores . They will also acquire hands -on experience with 
modern FPGA tools and platforms to implement, debug, and optimize complex digital systems.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Communication Concepts; Data and Voice Communications; Hardware Systems and 
Configurations; Network Topologies and Design Aspects; Protocols; Networking Local Area Networks; 
Network Security and Management; Emerging Trends in Communications. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: A communication network is one of the fastest-growing areas 
today. The course introduces the concepts and mechanisms underlying the modern telecommunication 
systems and networks. The course is designed in such a way that the course is accessible to students without 
any special technical background in this area. The OSI model is used as a framework to introduce different 
protocols and standards. The course will prepare the student for advanced courses in the areas of 
telecommunication switching systems, computer networks, internetworking, etc.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Introduction to IoT, Sensors and Actuators for IoT, Programming IoT end points, 
Communications and networking in IoT, Data management in IoT, Security issues in IoT, Emerging technologies. 
This course is discipline elective (DEL) for: Undergraduate level: B.E. (EEE), B.E (ECE), 
B.E. (E&I)/ dualites in those disciplines. For other discipline, it will be considered as an open elective (OPEL). 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This module is designed to provide students with solid technical knowledge and skills to build Internet of Things  
(IoT) systems. Internet of things has evolved due to convergence of multiple technologies - embedded systems, sensor 
technology, real-time data analytics, machine learning etc. Traditional fields of embedded systems, wire less sensor 
networks, control systems, automation (including home and building automation), and others all contribute to 
enabling the IoT. This course comprehensively covers various technologies and tools used for enabling IoT solutions. 
Knowledge of various topics required for building IoT prototypes like sensors  and actuators/ Communications and 
networking and data management is also imparted in this course. This course would also help the students understand 
the various IoT security challenges and solution to address them. The course will also give the students exposure to 
how various real world problems are being solved by IoT based solutions (like in applications for smart city, smart 
farming etc.). There would also be some hands on sessions where students would learn how to build and program IoT 
systems and make end-to- end solutions for different applications. Furthermore, assignments and projects in this 
course would help students build IoT prototypes and apply what they have learnt in the cours e to solve real world  
problems. 
 
3. Course learning Objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: 
a. Understand and explain the fundamental concepts, architectures, enabling technologies, communication protocols, 
data-management techniques, and security challenges associated with Internet of Things systems. 
b. Design and develop IoT-based solutions by integrating sensors, actuators, microcontrollers, communication 
networks, cloud platforms, and data-analytics tools. 
c. Apply practical programming and system-integration skills to build, test, and evaluate end-to-end IoT prototypes 
for addressing real-world applications such as smart cities, smart agriculture, healthcare, and industrial automation.

syllabus.text:
Introduction to IoT, Sensors and Actuators for IoT, Programming IoT end points, 
Communications and networking in IoT, Data management in IoT, Security issues in IoT, Emerging technologies. 
This course is discipline elective (DEL) for: Undergraduate level: B.E. (EEE), B.E (ECE), 
B.E. (E&I)/ dualites in those disciplines. For other discipline, it will be considered as an open elective (OPEL). 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This module is designed to provide students with solid technical knowledge and skills to build Internet of Things  
(IoT) systems. Internet of things has evolved due to convergence of multiple technologies - embedded systems, sensor 
technology, real-time data analytics, machine learning etc. Traditional fields of embedded systems, wire less sensor 
networks, control systems, automation (including home and building automation), and others all contribute to 
enabling the IoT. This course comprehensively covers various technologies and tools used for enabling IoT solutions. 
Knowledge of various topics required for building IoT prototypes like sensors  and actuators/ Communications and 
networking and data management is also imparted in this course. This course would also help the students understand 
the various IoT security challenges and solution to address them. The course will also give the students exposure to 
how various real world problems are being solved by IoT based solutions (like in applications for smart city, smart 
farming etc.). There would also be some hands on sessions where students would learn how to build and program IoT 
systems and make end-to- end solutions for different applications. Furthermore, assignments and projects in this 
course would help students build IoT prototypes and apply what they have learnt in the cours e to solve real world  
problems. 
 
3. Course learning Objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: 
a. Understand and explain the fundamental concepts, architectures, enabling technologies, communication protocols, 
data-management techniques, and security challenges associated with Internet of Things systems. 
b. Design and develop IoT-based solutions by integrating sensors, actuators, microcontrollers, communication 
networks, cloud platforms, and data-analytics tools. 
c. Apply practical programming and system-integration skills to build, test, and evaluate end-to-end IoT prototypes 
for addressing real-world applications such as smart cities, smart agriculture, healthcare, and industrial automation.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even 
some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the so -
called Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in th e previous compulsory course 
on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state 
variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of 
nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techn iques will be emphasized and 
also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments 
drawn from various engineering domains.  
2. Scopes and Objectives   
After completing this course the students will be able to 
1) Analyze various properties (E.g. stability) of linear and nonlinear dynamic systems 
2) Design linear state and output feedback controllers in time domain   
3) Design linear optimal controllers in both deterministic and stochastic domains  
4) Design Kalman Filter and Extended Kalman Filter (widely used signal processing tool)    
5) Design nonlinear state feedback controllers using backstepping algorithm   
6) Simplify higher order LTI models to lower order ones 
3. Prescribed Text/ Reference Books 
1. Control Systems by I.K. Nagrath and M. Gopal, New Age 
2. Control Systems Engineering by Norman Nise, John Wiley 
3. Modern Control Theory by M. Gopal, New Age  
4. Systems and Control by S.H. Zak, OUP 
5. Modern Control Design with Matlab and Simulink by Ashish Tewari, John Wiley

sources.text:
4. Course Plan:    
 
Module Lecture Sessions 
1. Linear Systems 
Modelling and Analysis 
(13L, 30%)  
 
 
 
L1: Overview of the course and how it takes the previous course forward 
L2-3: Review of state space modelling; State space and transfer function 
inter-conversion 
L4-6: Similarity transformation; Controllable, observable, diagonal and 
Jordan canonical forms (graphical and analytical methods) 
L7-8: Solution of state equation; Computation of state transition matrix 
by Laplace transform and Cayley-Hamilton methods 
L9: Discretization of continuous time state space model by step and 
impulse invariance methods 
L10-11: BIBO versus asymptotic stability; Controllability, observability, 
stabilizability, detectability  
L12-13: Introduction to model order reduction techniques: state 
space/modal/balanced truncation/residualization 
2. Nonlinear Systems 
Modelling and Analysis 
(9L, 20%) 
L14-15: Introduction to nonlinear systems: representations, examples; 
Hard nonlinearities 
L16-17: Jacobian linearization; Peculiarities of nonlinear systems; 
Introduction to bifurcation and chaos 
L18-19: Analysis of nonlinear systems: describing function method 
L20: Analysis of nonlinear systems: phase plane method 
L21-22: Stability analysis of nonlinear systems: Lyapunov’s indirect and 
direct methods and LaSalle’s invariance principle

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  This is the first  course on digital image processing. It begins with an 
introduction to the fundamentals of digital images and discusses the various discrete transformations, 
which are extensively used in image processing. It then goes on to discuss the different image 
processing techniques such as image enhancement, automatic image classification, and recognition. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  Digital Image Processing (DIP) involves the use of computer 
algorithms to perform operations on digital images to improve their quality, extract useful information, 
or prepare them for further analysis. The main objectives of DIP include enhancing image de tails for 
better visual interpretation, restoring corrupted images, compressing image data for efficient storage 
and transmission, and analyzing images for applications like medical diagnosis, satellite imaging, and 
object recognition. Its scope spans vari ous fields such as healthcare, agriculture, surveillance, remote 
sensing, and artificial intelligence, making it a vital tool in both scientific research and everyday 
technology.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: The course describes both theoretical and practical aspects of semiconductor 
fabrication technology. This course will take you on the journey of silica sand to silicon integrated circuit (IC), 
i.e., “making a chip”. Converting a single crystal of silicon into an IC requires several fabrication steps, such 
as epitaxy, oxidation, che mical vapor deposition, metallization, ion implantation, diffusion, etching, and 
lithography. All these process steps will be discussed. Further, the modeling of each processing step would be 
discussed in detail. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This course is designed to provide an introduction to the basic principles of semiconductor fabrication and to 
discuss various processing technologies. Fabrication of semiconductor chips is a joint venture by electrical 
engineers, chemical engineers, materials scientists, and physicists. This interdisciplinary course builds bridges 
across various disciplines.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:
Review of microwave communications and LOS systems; the various satellite orbits like GEO,
MEO, LEO; the satellite link analysis and design; the communication transponder system like
INSAT, INELSAT etc; the earth segment and earth station engineering; the transmission of analog
and digital signals through satellite and various modulation techniques employed; the multiple
access techniques like FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, DAMA, etc; the INSAT program; salient features of
INSAT – systems and services offered; satellite services offered by INTELSAT, INMARSAT and
future satellites like IRIDIUM etc; future trends in satellite communications.
2. Scope & Objectives of the Course:
This course introduces satellite communication systems, combining radio-wave propagation, or-
bital mechanics, satellite subsystems, modulation, and coding. Satellite link analysis and link-
budget design form the core, applied hands-on component of the course, reinforced through
in-class problem-solving sessions and selected simulation tasks. Students then study fixed-
assignment multiple-access techniques (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA) and briefly explore random-access
schemes, followed by applications in VSAT, mobile satellite, and GPS/DGPS. By the end of the
course, students will be able to analyze satellite communication systems, able to design satellite
links and evaluate their performance, develop and defend a link-budget analysis, and determine
satellite position/coverage for a given orbit.

syllabus.heading: Course Plan

sources.text:
5. Course Plan:
This undergraduate-level satellite communication course deals with the fundamentals of satellite
communications. The course comprises six modules: M1) Module 1 consists of an introduction,
historical developments, and research trends. M2) Module 2 covers satellite orbits, orbit elements,
orbital effects, and Friendship7 spacecraft. M3) Module 3 comprises satellite link parameters,
uplink, and downlink budget. M4) The fourth module consists of modulation, multiplexing, and
error control coding. M5) The fifth module covers multiple access techniques. M6) The last module
includes selected topics such as very small aperture terminal (VSAT), mobile sat (MSAT), the
global positioning system (GPS), differential GPS (DGPS) and recent trends and advances.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:
Review of microwave communications and LOS systems; the various satellite orbits like GEO,
MEO, LEO; the satellite link analysis and design; the communication transponder system like
INSAT, INELSAT etc; the earth segment and earth station engineering; the transmission of analog
and digital signals through satellite and various modulation techniques employed; the multiple
access techniques like FDMA, TDMA, CDMA, DAMA, etc; the INSAT program; salient features of
INSAT – systems and services offered; satellite services offered by INTELSAT, INMARSAT and
future satellites like IRIDIUM etc; future trends in satellite communications.
2. Scope & Objectives of the Course:
This course introduces satellite communication systems, combining radio-wave propagation, or-
bital mechanics, satellite subsystems, modulation, and coding. Satellite link analysis and link-
budget design form the core, applied hands-on component of the course, reinforced through
in-class problem-solving sessions and selected simulation tasks. Students then study fixed-
assignment multiple-access techniques (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA) and briefly explore random-access
schemes, followed by applications in VSAT, mobile satellite, and GPS/DGPS. By the end of the
course, students will be able to analyze satellite communication systems, able to design satellite
links and evaluate their performance, develop and defend a link-budget analysis, and determine
satellite position/coverage for a given orbit.

sources.text:
Lab Instructor  : Laveena Dadhich (RS)  
 
List of Experiments  
1. Design and analysis of microstrip lines: 
a. Varying width (W) and substrates (ε r)  plot Zo vs W for different ε r (at least 10 
points) 
b. Design load terminations: matched/unmatched with those of the microstrip 
line’s characteristic impedance  port and discrete impedance  
2. Emulation of inductive and capacitive loads with TX line (CST) and matching with stub for: 
a. Real-to-real termination  
b. Real to complex termination 
3. a. VNA calibration: Through, Open, Short, and Load termination.  
b. Determination of the S -matrix of a transmission line (2 -port) with VNA and validation with 
theory   
4. Design and development of matching networks (CST): 
a. Quarter wave (single section and multi-section) – single band 
b. Dual band 
c. Tri-band 
5. Design of planar microwave devices: directional coupler, attenuator, Wilkinson power divider, 
circulators  
6. Measurement of power received for an antenna setup with VNA and a Spectrum analyzer: 
a. Horn antenna 
b. Patch antenna 
7. Familiarization with Microwave Bench Setup and equipment: Characterization of Reflex 
Klystron Modes  
8. Determination of VSWR, Reflection Coefficient, and Frequency of Operation with Reflex 
Klystron                                 
                                                                                                      Dinesh Rano

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Introduction to radio frequency engineering; advantages; various frequency bands; applications; Microwave 
passive components and hig h frequency modeling; Microwave network analysis:  scattering parameters and 
Signal flow graph; vector network analyzer-dynamic range and IF bandwidth; Transmission lines; microstrip 
lines; impedance matching techniques -transmission line based and lumped c ircuit approach and layout 
generation. Power dividers and couplers, RF filter design; Filter scaling and transformation; Filter 
implementation using microstrip lines and lumped components; Amplifier design; noise, harmonic distortion, 
and intercept point analysis, amplifier design for gain and noise figure; oscillator design, one -port and two- 
port oscillator design, phase noise of oscillator, introduction to EMI and EMC, recent trends. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
Identify basic RF devices/components and their applications, understand common rules of thumb in RF design, 
use scattering matrix for RF network analysis, design planar transmission lines, design impedance -matching 
circuits, use the Smith chart for impedan ce matching, implement passive RF devices in planar technology, 
design passive RF devices with RF CAD tools, learn the use of a vector network analyzer for RF 
measurements, learn the basic principles of RF amplifier

sources.text:
Lab Instructor  : Laveena Dadhich (RS)  
 
List of Experiments  
1. Design and analysis of microstrip lines: 
a. Varying width (W) and substrates (ε r)  plot Zo vs W for different ε r (at least 10 
points) 
b. Design load terminations: matched/unmatched with those of the microstrip 
line’s characteristic impedance  port and discrete impedance  
2. Emulation of inductive and capacitive loads with TX line (CST) and matching with stub for: 
a. Real-to-real termination  
b. Real to complex termination 
3. a. VNA calibration: Through, Open, Short, and Load termination.  
b. Determination of the S -matrix of a transmission line (2 -port) with VNA and validation with 
theory   
4. Design and development of matching networks (CST): 
a. Quarter wave (single section and multi-section) – single band 
b. Dual band 
c. Tri-band 
5. Design of planar microwave devices: directional coupler, attenuator, Wilkinson power divider, 
circulators  
6. Measurement of power received for an antenna setup with VNA and a Spectrum analyzer: 
a. Horn antenna 
b. Patch antenna 
7. Familiarization with Microwave Bench Setup and equipment: Characterization of Reflex 
Klystron Modes  
8. Determination of VSWR, Reflection Coefficient, and Frequency of Operation with Reflex 
Klystron                                 
                                                                                                      Dinesh Rano

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Introduction to radio frequency engineering; advantages; various frequency bands; applications; Microwave 
passive components and hig h frequency modeling; Microwave network analysis:  scattering parameters and 
Signal flow graph; vector network analyzer-dynamic range and IF bandwidth; Transmission lines; microstrip 
lines; impedance matching techniques -transmission line based and lumped c ircuit approach and layout 
generation. Power dividers and couplers, RF filter design; Filter scaling and transformation; Filter 
implementation using microstrip lines and lumped components; Amplifier design; noise, harmonic distortion, 
and intercept point analysis, amplifier design for gain and noise figure; oscillator design, one -port and two- 
port oscillator design, phase noise of oscillator, introduction to EMI and EMC, recent trends. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
Identify basic RF devices/components and their applications, understand common rules of thumb in RF design, 
use scattering matrix for RF network analysis, design planar transmission lines, design impedance -matching 
circuits, use the Smith chart for impedan ce matching, implement passive RF devices in planar technology, 
design passive RF devices with RF CAD tools, learn the use of a vector network analyzer for RF 
measurements, learn the basic principles of RF amplifier

Modelling an embedded System, Design using ARM Processors - Core v7 , Cortex M, Buses, I/O interface - 
Basic, Communication and Advance, Embedded Software Design, Embedded Software: Tasks, Task 
Management RTS, Advanced Embedded System Design Concepts such as Power management, Fault Tolerant 
System Design, Basics of H/W - S/W codesign, SoC based design etc, Memory Types, Cache, MMU/MPU 
basics, On-chip/off-chip bus architectures, Hardware Accelerators. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
The course intends to introduce the various components of an embedded system and embedded system design 
considerations. The course also deals with processor architectures, on -chip & off - chip protocols, 
programming techniques, performance analysis, and optimization techniques used in embedded system 
development. This course introduces the students to standard Embedded System Development tools and gives 
hands-on experience in developing various embedded applications. 
 
No Course Objective 
CL01 Understanding of Hardware and Software Components of a typical Embedded System 
CL02 Understanding the challenges in “ System Level Design” and developing system design skills 
CL03 Develop programming skills and practical expertise in designing, debugging, and developing 
small-scale and medium-scale Embedded systems 
CL04 Introduction to advanced topics of research in the field of Embedded Systems

1.1. Introduction

instructors.label: Instructor-in-charge

sources.text:
Instructor-in-charge: Dr. Ritesh Vyas 
 
Scope of the course: 
The rise of machine learning (ML) has introduced many opportunities in the design of 
electronic systems. This course provides a requisite conceptual foundation of ML and 
contextual application of ML techniques for improving the performance of electronic systems. 
The course introduces the major approaches to ML such as supervised, unsupervised, semi-
supervised, and reinforcement learning. The course also lays emphasis on various deep learning 
techniques and their application to various types of electronic systems/sub -systems (e.g. 
control-dominated systems, NLP systems, vision-based systems, communication systems, 
embedded systems, IoTs). Additionally, the course covers advance topics in ML such as multi-
modal, multi-task learning as well as transfer learning. The course discusses the challenges in 
implementation of ML techniques, complexity analysis of the ML architectures for hardware 
implementation, efficient architectures, and various topologies used for implementation. 
 
Outcomes:  
• Students should be able to apply ML techniques to model, design, validate, and 
optimize embedded electronic systems in their area of interest. 
• Develop the skills and practical exposure in modeling, developing, and debugging ML-
based systems. 
• Develop the foundation required to explore advanced topics of research in ML.

electronic systems. This course provides a requisite conceptual foundation of ML and 
contextual application of ML techniques for improving the performance of electronic systems.

supervised, and reinforcement learning. The course also lays emphasis on various deep learning 
techniques and their application to various types of electronic systems/sub -systems (e.g.

implementation of ML techniques, complexity analysis of the ML architectures for hardware 
implementation, efficient architectures, and various topologies used for implementation.

optimize embedded electronic systems in their area of interest.

Course Description : 
This course will introduce the general concepts related to real-time systems from introduction, to designing 
a real-time system (RTS). It will deal will a reference model of an RTS which can be applied to any RTS. It will 
also teach the scheduling algorithms, resource management techniques, issues in hardware and software 
design, Real -Time Operating System (RTOS), advanced concepts of software design and validation 
techniques for these systems.

Course Title             : Signal Theory and Optimization

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description:  
Probability theory and random variables; joint, conditional, and marginal distributions; functions of 
random variables; moments, expectation, and statistical inequalities; introduction to random processes; 
stationarity, autocorrelation, ergodicity, and power spectral density; basic concepts of linear algebra: 
vector spaces, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations, spectral decomposition; 
matrix factorizations including SVD, LU, and QR; positive definite matrices; orthogonal projections 
in Hilbert spaces; introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and 
constrained optimization; Lagrange multipliers, Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and 
numerical optimization techniques.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
I. Course Description: 
This course introduces the principles, design, and applications of optoelectronic devices. The course 
begins with a description of the interaction of light with semiconductor materials in a p -n junction 
configuration. This includes the phenomena of absorption, electroluminescence, and stimulated 
emission. The distinction between direct and indirect semiconductor materials is noted. Basic 
devices are then described: photodiodes, light-emitting diodes (LEDs), semiconductor optical 
amplifiers, and laser diodes . Array detectors, including complementary metal -oxide-semiconductor 
(CMOS) and charge -coupled devices (CCD) arrays, and array LEDs are then introduced. Basic 
specifications and applications of each of these devices are described, including solar cells, imaging 
with array detectors, and LED displays.

sources.text:

SI. 
No. 
Module Topic Outcome(s) 
1 
Physics of 
semiconductors 
(6 hours) 
Review of semiconductor concepts, 
carrier transport, and energy bands.  
Direct vs. Indirect bandgap 
semiconductors E-k diagrams).  P-n 
junction principles, heterojunctions, 
and energy band diagrams under bias. 
Map energy band diagrams for direct and indirect 
bandgap semiconductors using E -k diagrams to 
predict radiative efficiency.

Light-Emitting 
Diodes (LEDs) 
(8 hours) 
Core principles of 
electroluminescence, efficiencies, and 
output spectrum.  High-intensity 
quantum well LEDs and modern 
materials.  White LEDs, phosphors, 
and driver electronics, Organic LEDs 
(OLEDs), Quantum Dot LEDs 
(QLEDs) 
Explain the role of quantum wells and modern 
semiconductor materials in high -brightness LED 
configurations. Evaluate the operating 
mechanisms of phosphor -converted white LEDs, 
OLEDs, and QLEDs for display and lighting 
applications. 
3 
Laser Diodes & 
Optical 
Amplifiers (6 
hours) 
Laser oscillations: threshold gain 
coefficient and gain bandwidth.  
Steady-state semiconductor rate 
equations.  Single-frequency lasers 
and Vertical Cavity Surface Emitting 
Lasers (VCSELs).  Semiconductor 
Optical Amplifiers (SOAs). 
Formulate and solve steady -state rate equations to 
determine photon and carrier densities. Critique 
the design and structural benefits of single -
frequency lasers, VCSELs, and Semiconductor 
Optical Amplifiers (SOAs). 
4 
Flexible 
substrates and 
display devices 
(6 hours) 
Flexible silicon and SoI wafers, 
Techniques for fabricating flexible Si-
substrates, Thin Film Transistors 
(TFTs), TFT-LCD Displays 
Identify engineering constraints and candidate 
materials for flexible, stretchable, and wearable 
substrates. Assess the mechanical and electrical 
reliability of optoelectronic materials under 
mechanical stress.

Photodetectors 
& Photovoltaics

Photovoltaic devices and solar cell 
efficiencies.  Noise parameters in 
photodetection. 
Assess noise contributions (shot noise, thermal 
noise) to determine the Signal -to-Noise Ratio 
(SNR) and Noise Equivalent Power (NEP) of a 
detector. Analyze the photovoltaic effect and 
extraction efficiency parameters that dictate solar 
cell performance.
