syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
This course covers analysis of series and parallel resonant converters, load dependent properties of resonant converters 
with ZVS/ZCS boundary. Operation of these converters for Zero-current Switching and Zero-Voltage switching is 
discussed in detail. The concept of resonance is extended to analyze the soft switching mechanism of semiconductor 
devices Diode, MOSFET and IGBT to reduce the switching loss and possible mitigation of EMI. The zero -current-
switching and the zero-voltage-switching quasi resonant switch cell is discussed for full bridge converter. Design example 
of zero-current-switching and zero-voltage switching class E-inverter is also covered in this course. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
a. Understand the concept of resonant tank network 
b. Analyze the dependence of ZVS/ZCS boundary on load resistance 
c. Design ZVS/ZCS switch cell for DC-DC converter 
d. Analysis of switching loss and EMI under soft switching

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: This course covers advance power electronic circuits which includes DC-DC converters, Rectifiers and 
Inverters. Steady state analysis of these converters is discussed in detail with emphasis on proper selection of devices and magnetic 
components. Mathematical modelling of converter transfer function using various approaches is also included for controller design 
of these converters. Experiments are designed to understand the working of these power electronic circuits supported with 
MATLAB/SIMULINK based simulation platform. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
a. Understand the main elements of power electronic circuits 
b. Steady-state analysis of basic power electronic circuits like DC-DC converters, rectifiers and inverters 
c. Derivation of AC small signal model and transfer functions of power converters 
d. Experimental validation Basic power converter circuits 
e. Development of one new converter for selected applications

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  This ME course is meant for equipping students with knowledge of 
prevalent power quality issues in the modern power distribution system, their causes and classifications 
covering voltage and current based power quality problems such as sag, swell, unbalance, harmonics 
and poor power factor. Various standards on power qu ality and their monitoring techniques are also 
covered. The course also majorly deals with power quality compensation techniques including both 
passive and active compensation, their design, analysis and modeling. The control techniques for active 
power compensators and active filters are also discussed. The lab component is designed to enrich 
students’ knowledge of power quality with practical hands on and simulation exercises.  
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  A ME course focusing on electric power qual ity typically 
covers the analysis, mitigation, and improvement of power quality issues, including voltage variations, 
harmonics, and other disturbances, preparing graduates for careers in power utilities and industries. 
The objectives of this course are designed to help students to: 
a. Understand various power quality issues and their impact. 
b. Learn about power and power factor in single-phase and three-phase systems.  
c. Study conventional and active compensation techniques for power factor correction and 
load voltage regulation 
d. Gain knowledge of active filter techniques for harmonics elimination.  
e. Understand power quality improvement in power supplies, drive systems, and renewable 
energy systems. 
Learning outcomes of the course have been incorporated in the course plan on next page.

5. Course Plan:   
   
Module No. & Name Lecture 
Sessions References Learning Outcomes 
1. Fundamentals of Power 
Quality 
L1-L5 
T1 (1.1-1.6, 
2.1-2.6), T2 
(1.1-1.4, 2.1-
2.12) 
Introduction to power quality problems related to 
voltage variations, waveform distortion, low power 
factor etc., their causes and effects. Power quality 
terminologies and definitions, industry standards, 
monitoring. 
2. Non-linear Loads and 
Harmonics 
L6-L9 
T1 (7.1-7.6), 
T2 (5.1-5.10), 
R1 (3.2) 
Introduction to non-linear loads and problem of 
harmonics caused by them, their analysis, modeling and 
simulation. Calculation of active & reactive powers and 
power factor for non-linear loads 
3. Passive Compensation 
Techniques 
L10-L12 T1 (3.1-3.6) 
 
Introduction to passive shunt and series compensators, 
their classification, principle of operation, analysis, 
design and simulation. 
4. Active Shunt 
Compensation 
Techniques L13-L18 T1 (4.1-4.6) 
Introduction to shunt active compensators- 
DSTATCOMs, their classification, principle of 
operation, analysis, design, modeling control techniques 
and simulation. 
5. Active Series 
Compensation 
Techniques L19-L22 T1 (5.1-5.6) 
Introduction to series active compensators- DVRs, their 
classification, principle of operation, analysis, design, 
modeling control techniques and simulation. 
6. Unified Power Quality 
Compensators 
L23-L26 T1 (6.1-6.6) 
Introduction to unified compensators- combining shunt 
and series active compensators (UPQC), their 
classification, principle of operation, analysis, design, 
control techniques and simulation. Advantages and 
disadvantages of UPQC. 
7. Passive power filters 
L27-L29 T1 (8.1-8.8), 
T2 (6.1-6.8) 
Passive power filters for harmonic mitigation, their 
classification, principle of operation, analysis, design, 
modeling and simulation. Problem of parallel resonance 
in passive filters and its mitigation 
8. Active Power Filters 
L30-L36 T1 (9.1-9.6, 
10.1-10.6) 
Introduction to shunt and series active power filters for 
harmonic mitigation, their classification, principle of 
operation, analysis, design, modeling, control 
techniques, and simulation. Introduction to hybrid active 
power filters. 
9. Power Quality 
Applications and Related 
Topics L37-L40 
T2 (9.3-9.8, 
10.1-10.5), 
class notes. 
Power quality issues and solutions in areas like DC 
power supplies, renewable energy systems, industrial 
applications, electric vehicle charging stations and smart 
grids.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  This ME course is meant for equipping students with knowledge of 
prevalent power quality issues in the modern power distribution system, their causes and classifications 
covering voltage and current based power quality problems such as sag, swell, unbalance, harmonics 
and poor power factor. Various standards on power qu ality and their monitoring techniques are also 
covered. The course also majorly deals with power quality compensation techniques including both 
passive and active compensation, their design, analysis and modeling. The control techniques for active 
power compensators and active filters are also discussed. The lab component is designed to enrich 
students’ knowledge of power quality with practical hands on and simulation exercises.  
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  A ME course focusing on electric power qual ity typically 
covers the analysis, mitigation, and improvement of power quality issues, including voltage variations, 
harmonics, and other disturbances, preparing graduates for careers in power utilities and industries. 
The objectives of this course are designed to help students to: 
a. Understand various power quality issues and their impact. 
b. Learn about power and power factor in single-phase and three-phase systems.  
c. Study conventional and active compensation techniques for power factor correction and 
load voltage regulation 
d. Gain knowledge of active filter techniques for harmonics elimination.  
e. Understand power quality improvement in power supplies, drive systems, and renewable 
energy systems. 
Learning outcomes of the course have been incorporated in the course plan on next page.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Semiconductor fundamentals for Nanotechnology, Introduction to low dimensional nano-structures and 
Quantum Mechanics ,Scaling and nanoelectronics, Nano electronic device materials and circuits, Strain 
engineering and high speed quantum electronic devices, Optical properties of nano-structures, Linear and 
non linear effects of optical materials and structures, Nano photonic devices, Electronic Devices based on 
nano structures in evolution of Silicon Base Devices, Integrated photo electronic devices and systems and 
its applications, New Trends in Nano devices and technology. 
 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This course provides a blend of electronic and photonic fundamentals and their applications to the fast 
moving technology involved in high -speed electronics, optical electronics and optical communication 
systems in terms of nano s tructures. Electronics and Photonics are becoming increasingly important as 
limitations of speed, size and bandwidth affect many electronic devices and systems. Moreover, 
integration of electronics and photonics becomes an important issue related to modern  technical aspects 
like optical interconnects, integrated optical circuits etc. Here the fundamentals of semiconductors, 
quantum structures and transport properties related to quantum structures will be first discussed. That will 
be followed by electronic and optical properties and details of strain engineering. Finally all these basic 
concepts will be applied in understanding modern and photonic and electronic devices useful for 
engineering applications. Students will also be encouraged to learn hands -on-training in analysis/ 
simulation of some electronic-photonic devices using MATLAB/ SILVACO TCAD software.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Semiconductor fundamentals for Nanotechnology, Introduction to low dimensional nano-structures and 
Quantum Mechanics ,Scaling and nanoelectronics, Nano electronic device materials and circuits, Strain 
engineering and high speed quantum electronic devices, Optical properties of nano-structures, Linear and 
non linear effects of optical materials and structures, Nano photonic devices, Electronic Devices based on 
nano structures in evolution of Silicon Base Devices, Integrated photo electronic devices and systems and 
its applications, New Trends in Nano devices and technology. 
 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This course provides a blend of electronic and photonic fundamentals and their applications to the fast 
moving technology involved in high -speed electronics, optical electronics and optical communication 
systems in terms of nano s tructures. Electronics and Photonics are becoming increasingly important as 
limitations of speed, size and bandwidth affect many electronic devices and systems. Moreover, 
integration of electronics and photonics becomes an important issue related to modern  technical aspects 
like optical interconnects, integrated optical circuits etc. Here the fundamentals of semiconductors, 
quantum structures and transport properties related to quantum structures will be first discussed. That will 
be followed by electronic and optical properties and details of strain engineering. Finally all these basic 
concepts will be applied in understanding modern and photonic and electronic devices useful for 
engineering applications. Students will also be encouraged to learn hands -on-training in analysis/ 
simulation of some electronic-photonic devices using MATLAB/ SILVACO TCAD software.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Evolution of wireless cellular technologies to 5G and beyond, review of matrix and signal theory for 
communication applications, introduction to stochastic geometry for performance analysis of wireless 
networks, D2D communications- modeling and analysis, cooperative communications-buffer-aided relaying 
and performance analysis, modulation and multiple access techniques-NOMA, OTFS, OAM. Introduction to 
potential technologies for beyond 5G/6G communications: IRS, molecular communications, and AI in 
wireless communications. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
a) This course aims to introduce the students to the advances in wireless communications and expose 
them to the research options available for applications in the real -world implementation of the next - 
generation wireless networks. 
b) The course will introduce the students to current trends in the wireless industry with a specific focus 
on the 5G and beyond 5G communication networks. 
c) The course aims to equip students with tools for designing the engineering aspect s of wireless 
communications. 
d) New techniques envisaged to be a part of the next -generation wireless networks, like D2D 
communications, NOMA, OTFS, and stochastic geometry applied to wireless communications, to 
name a few, will be covered to make the student industry and research-ready.

amplifiers and applications.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even 
some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the so -
called Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in th e previous compulsory course 
on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state 
variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of 
nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techn iques will be emphasized and 
also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments 
drawn from various engineering domains.  
2. Scopes and Objectives   
After completing this course the students will be able to 
1) Analyze various properties (E.g. stability) of linear and nonlinear dynamic systems 
2) Design linear state and output feedback controllers in time domain   
3) Design linear optimal controllers in both deterministic and stochastic domains  
4) Design Kalman Filter and Extended Kalman Filter (widely used signal processing tool)    
5) Design nonlinear state feedback controllers using backstepping algorithm   
6) Simplify higher order LTI models to lower order ones 
3. Prescribed Text/ Reference Books 
1. Control Systems by I.K. Nagrath and M. Gopal, New Age 
2. Control Systems Engineering by Norman Nise, John Wiley 
3. Modern Control Theory by M. Gopal, New Age  
4. Systems and Control by S.H. Zak, OUP 
5. Modern Control Design with Matlab and Simulink by Ashish Tewari, John Wiley

syllabus.heading: Course Plan

sources.text:
4. Course Plan:    
 
Module Lecture Sessions 
1. Linear Systems 
Modelling and Analysis 
(13L, 30%)  
 
 
 
L1: Overview of the course and how it takes the previous course forward 
L2-3: Review of state space modelling; State space and transfer function 
inter-conversion 
L4-6: Similarity transformation; Controllable, observable, diagonal and 
Jordan canonical forms (graphical and analytical methods) 
L7-8: Solution of state equation; Computation of state transition matrix 
by Laplace transform and Cayley-Hamilton methods 
L9: Discretization of continuous time state space model by step and 
impulse invariance methods 
L10-11: BIBO versus asymptotic stability; Controllability, observability, 
stabilizability, detectability  
L12-13: Introduction to model order reduction techniques: state 
space/modal/balanced truncation/residualization 
2. Nonlinear Systems 
Modelling and Analysis 
(9L, 20%) 
L14-15: Introduction to nonlinear systems: representations, examples; 
Hard nonlinearities 
L16-17: Jacobian linearization; Peculiarities of nonlinear systems; 
Introduction to bifurcation and chaos 
L18-19: Analysis of nonlinear systems: describing function method 
L20: Analysis of nonlinear systems: phase plane method 
L21-22: Stability analysis of nonlinear systems: Lyapunov’s indirect and 
direct methods and LaSalle’s invariance principle

syllabus.heading: Course Content

sources.text:
Course Content 
Introduction to hydrosphere, atmosphere, geosphere and anthrosphere (tangible human interaction space), 
with chemical interactions, deterioration (pollution and degradation/depletion) and remediation processes

sources.text:
Course Description: 
The course will provide an overview of the different aspects of the environment and the chemistry integrally 
involved in it. Broad description of the constituents of the environment namely the hydrosphere, the 
atmosphere, the geosphere and the anthrosphere (tangible human interaction space) will be provided with 
emphasis on the chemical interactions involved in e ach of them in their respective formation, balanced 
existence, deterioration (pollution and degradation/ depletion) and remediation processes etc.  The course 
will be essential to gaining an understanding of our environment and the chemistry behind the proc esses 
occurring within, with relevance to the current industrialized  ecology. The course will also provide an 
overview of environmental biotechnology , emphasising biotechnological tools, such as microbial, genetic, 
and biochemical mechanisms involved in ecosystem function, pollution, and remediation. The course will 
cover sustainable biotechnological interventions in waste treatment, bioenergy production, and pollution 
control. It is designed to build a foundational understanding of how biotechnology inte grates with 
environmental systems, enabling learners to address environmental degradation in the context of modern 
industrialized ecology.

The course will be broadly divided based on the three major components as hydrosphere, atmosphere and 
geosphere. Learning objectives for each of the broad topic s as discussed in the course plan has been 
described along with – what the learner should be able to do by studying these.

sources.text: Course Title : [Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting]
Course Title : [Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting]

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: 
 Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not  
only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also  
communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize  
transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails 
two important and interrelated aspects, i.e., 
a. Recording transactions, and 
b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc. 
Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing 
financial statements. 
The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules  
of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial 
balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership,  
credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the  
statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold,  
recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets. 
This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students 
and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from 
Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and  
financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced  
courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent  
semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance.  
Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the  
field of finance.

Course Title : Security Analysis and Portfolio Management

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected 
problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold. 
The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return 
profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental, 
quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy, 
industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation 
forms a major component of this course. 
Another important aspect of the course is on modern portfolio concepts, where the criterion changes: 
a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the 
whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the 
construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance.

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected 
problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold. 
The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return 
profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental, 
quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy, 
industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation 
forms a major component of this course. 
Another important aspect of the course is on modern portfolio concepts, where the criterion changes: 
a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the 
whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the 
construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as 
a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial 
decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate 
level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic 
experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of 
Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by 
the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm. 
In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements, 
the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of 
firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other 
are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available 
to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with 
uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of 
fault lines in the financial markets. 
To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress 
suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More 
importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C -suite 
managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm 
must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment, 
investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing 
policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy. 
The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital, 
investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and 
sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies.

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: 
This course focuses on the concept of financial risk in modern finance. Despite market 
volatility and irrational exuberance, effective risk quantification and management remain 
crucial. Regulators have imposed safeguards to curb excessive risk -taking by financial 
institutions. As a result, risk management has become a core function in the finance industry. 
The course  is designed to prepare students for the growing demand in financial risk 
management roles. 
Financial risk (which includes interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign exchange risk and 
portfolio risk), Application of Asset price Theory, CAPM and Modern Portfo lio Theory, 
Multifactor models of risk and return, Capital adequacy, BASEL Norms; Comprehensive 
Capital Analysis and Review, Basel Committee on Banking Supervision guidelines, Value at 
Risk (VaR), VaR from regulator perspective, Responsive VaR Model, Addre ssing VaR 
weakness, Back testing  Concepts - Checking the Strength of VaR Model, Issues with the 
Standard VaR models, Risk Not in VaR (RNIV) to VaR migration of risk, Volatility Clustering, 
Quantifying and Modeling volatilities, Hedging techniques, Options Greeks, Managing Risk 
with Derivatives.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
 
 Concepts of State, Nation, Rights and Duties, Civil Society, Democracy, Citizenship and Justice. 
 Ideologies of Modern Politics : Social Contractualism, Liberalism, Socialism, Communism, 
Maoism, Anarchism, Secularism. 
 Selected Readings from key texts of leading thinkers in the History of Modern Western Political 
Philosophy including Machiavelli’s Prince, Hobbes’ Leviathan, Locke’s Second Treatise of 
government, Rousseau’s Discourse on the origin of inequality , Marx and Engels’ Communist 
Manifesto. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This Course introduces certain select concepts of Politics that are relevant to the Modern/ 
Contemporary period. The course helps in unravelling the contexts from which these concepts emerged 
through a study of ideologies as well as first-hand reading of k ey texts in the history of political 
thought. 
This course prepares the students to be informed active citizens. The design and its execution 
emphasize the comprehension of political thinking, the application of communication and analytical 
skills, and the understanding of human diversity. 
 
Modern political concepts enhance the knowledge of the political science discipline by offering the 
conceptual vocabulary along with various methods of inquiry. This course not only increases students’ 
knowledge of the hi story of classical and modern political thought but also enlightens them with the 
fundamental values and ethical issues contested in politics over time. This course informs about the 
alternative moral and ethical frameworks for (re)interpreting and evaluat ing contemporary political 
discourses.

Course Title              : Environment, Development and Climate Change (EDCC)

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  This course focuses on the concepts of environ ment, development, and climate 
change in the contemporary world. The nature and causes of environmental problems in developing and 
developed countries will be explored. Attention is given to both the causes and solutions of environmental 
problems and the role of state and non-state actors interacting at local, national and global scales. The goal 
of this course is for the learners to app reciate the people -environment relations and to understand the 
anthropocentric dynamics of development and climate change. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The objective of the course is to make the students aware of the 
debates and issues relating to sustainable development and climate change, so as to sufficiently challenge 
them to come up with practical solutions. The course covers theory and practice at the global and local 
levels and examines the contemporary policy and practice regarding environment, development and 
climate change.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  This course focuses on the concept of development, development theories and  
practices in the modern world. Interplay between theory and practice and the outcome of this relationship are 
also explored in the syllabus. The course pro vides an overview of development thinking from ‘classical’  
development ideas to alternative and post development theories. The course then attempts to critically review 
contemporary debates about development, including the link between the current world order and the  
Development goals of the developing countries.  
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The objective of the course is to make the students aware of the 
debates and issues relating to development and post development. The course covers development theory 
and practice at the global and local levels and examines the practice in contemporary times.  
. Text Books: John Rapley (2010), Understanding Development: Theory and Practice in the Third World 
Viva Books. (Reading material will be given by the IC through classroom portal)

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  The course would introduce the stu dents to the ever changing dynamics  of Mass 
Media with its evolutionary and operational details.  The course would impart a broad knowledge of the 
developments, operations, types and impact of mass media. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
 
 To lay a foundation for students and give them the basis of conceptual and practical skills in the 
broad area of mass communication.  
 To develop a range of skills that includes research, writing, editing and presentation for news and 
strategic communication in print, audio and online.  
 To develop an understanding about the working of Mass media at the macro and micro levels by 
covering diverse range of Media such as Cinema, Social Media and Digital media.

sources.text:
1. Course description: The course is planned to give a comprehensive working 
knowledge of Advertising and Marketing communication and how they inter-relate. 
It offers modules, cas e studies and do -it your own assignment opportunities. The 
main feature of the course is that it is constantly evolving, keeping itself relevant to 
the needs of the advertising industry. Today’s student is expected to understand all 
the major marketing fun ctions: advertising, its process, integrated marketing 
communication involving across multimedia: podcast/podcasts, newspaper, 
magazine, television, and via Internet. It aims to enable the students to familiarize 
the advertising communication process and h ow it works in relation to market and 
the consumers.

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Principles of creative writing, stimulating creative activity, techniques of creating images, constructing 
events and creating characters, writing short stories, digital storytelling and multimodal narratives, plays 
and poems, adaptation of creative writing across digital and social media, writing critical essays on works 
of art, AI and digital writing tools, authorship and ethics 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
The objective of the course is to familiarize students with the nature and functioning of creative writing. 
Besides basic tenets of creative writing, the course will not only encourage the students to acquire 
techniques of constructing events, characters, writing poems, short stories and one act plays but also 
develop in them the ability to appreciate writings of all sorts. References to the related and contemporary 
works will be made from time to time during discussion and workshop.

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Introduction to, Importance and scope of Current Affairs; Domains of Current Affairs-Political, Social, Religious, 
Scientific, Developmental, etc.;Issues in Current Affairs-Controversial, Non-controversial, Neutral; Sources of 
Information in Current Affairs-newspapers, Magazines, Posters, Pamphlets, Manifestoes, recently published books, 
etc.; Reading: Skimming & Scanning, Extensive vs. Intensive, comprehension;Understanding current issues, events and 
information;  Interpreting current issues, events and information; Opinion formation-factors and materials influencing 
opinion formation;Balancing and expressing opinion.  
 
2. Scope and Objective of the course: 
 
The objectives of the course are to instill in students the habit of keeping themselves updated on a host of 
issues that relate not only to an individual but the society at large and also to inculcate among the students 
the skills of reading, understanding, interpreting and forming an opinion on national and international events 
and issues of different nature and of various domains. 
3. LearningOutcomes: 
 
Having successfully completed all the modules of the course, students will be able to 
 
a. Read about, listen to, interpret and understand current issues covered in print, 
visual and electronic media 
b. Analyze an issue from various perspectives and understand their implications for 
an individual, a nation and the society at large 
c. Identify ideological biases in people’s opinion 
d. Form informed opinion on any given issue 
e. Express opinion in an effective manner

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description 
Goals of Public Speaking, differences and similarities between Public Speaking and General Purpose 
Speaking, Role of Critical Thinking in Successful Public Speaking, Speaker’s Credibility; Different phases 
of Nervousness, dealing with Nervousness; Non - Verbal Communication, Using Body and Voice for 
communication, paralinguistic features; Using visual aids; Speech Writing and delivering - Effective 
Introductions and Conclusions; Speeches for Special Occasions; Team Presentations; Group Discussion 
and Job Interviews 
2. Scope and Objectives of the Course 
The course aims to familiarize students with the art of public speaking and help them become confident, 
ethical, and effective speakers in academic and professional contexts. Students will learn to manage public 
speaking anxiety, construct logical arguments, organize speeches, and deliver presentations using appropriate 
content, structure, language, paralinguistic features, kinesics, and visual aids. 
The revised course also enables students to use AI-assisted tools in a limited and responsible manner for idea 
generation, outline development, rehearsal feedback, and slide improvement, without replacing independent 
thinking or original expression. Students will be encouraged to assess AI output critically for accuracy,  
audience suitability, bias, and ethical use. 
3. Classroom Methodology 
The classroom methodology includes lectures, group and pair work, practical activities, guided rehearsal, 
and performance-based tasks. The course remains strongly practice -oriented and dev elops speaking skills 
through JAMs, extempore speaking, storytelling, parliamentary debates, group discussions, interviews, and 
presentation tasks. 
Video clips and model speeches will be used for illustration. In addition, selected classroom activities may  
include AI-supported speech brainstorming, AI-assisted audience adaptation tasks, and guided reflection on 
AI-generated feedback, while preserving the same teacher-led, practice-based format intact.

Video clips and model speeches will be used for illustration. In addition, selected classroom activities may  
include AI-supported speech brainstorming, AI-assisted audience adaptation tasks, and guided reflection on 
AI-generated feedback, while preserving the same teacher-led, practice-based format intact.

syllabus.text:
Goals of Public Speaking, differences and similarities between Public Speaking and General Purpose 
Speaking, Role of Critical Thinking in Successful Public Speaking, Speaker’s Credibility; Different phases 
of Nervousness, dealing with Nervousness; Non - Verbal Communication, Using Body and Voice for 
communication, paralinguistic features; Using visual aids; Speech Writing and delivering - Effective 
Introductions and Conclusions; Speeches for Special Occasions; Team Presentations; Group Discussion 
and Job Interviews 
2. Scope and Objectives of the Course 
The course aims to familiarize students with the art of public speaking and help them become confident, 
ethical, and effective speakers in academic and professional contexts. Students will learn to manage public 
speaking anxiety, construct logical arguments, organize speeches, and deliver presentations using appropriate 
content, structure, language, paralinguistic features, kinesics, and visual aids. 
The revised course also enables students to use AI-assisted tools in a limited and responsible manner for idea 
generation, outline development, rehearsal feedback, and slide improvement, without replacing independent 
thinking or original expression. Students will be encouraged to assess AI output critically for accuracy,  
audience suitability, bias, and ethical use. 
3. Classroom Methodology 
The classroom methodology includes lectures, group and pair work, practical activities, guided rehearsal, 
and performance-based tasks. The course remains strongly practice -oriented and dev elops speaking skills 
through JAMs, extempore speaking, storytelling, parliamentary debates, group discussions, interviews, and 
presentation tasks. 
Video clips and model speeches will be used for illustration. In addition, selected classroom activities may  
include AI-supported speech brainstorming, AI-assisted audience adaptation tasks, and guided reflection on 
AI-generated feedback, while preserving the same teacher-led, practice-based format intact.

Course Title                : Introduction to Conflict Management

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: Nature and dynamics of conflict; characteristics of conflict; theories of 
conflict; reasons and sources of conflict; value of conflict in social change; different 
approaches to addressing and managing conflict; conflict analysis through socio-economic 
class; class-based dimensions of conflict; culture and globalization perspectives; role of 
culture in propagating conflict; role of globalization in nation-state conflict; workplace and 
organizational conflict dynamics; conformity theories and conflict; power of 
communication; identity-based perspectives on conflict; AI, technology, and conflict 
resolution; algorithmic and digital dimensions of conflict; negotiation techniques; 
mitigation and resolution techniques; conflict management styles. 
 
 
2.    Scope and Objective of the Course: 
To develop the knowledge and professional skills necessary to facilitate resolution of conflicts. 
Emphasis would be laid on skills and specific techniques to resolve inter -personal, 
organizational and community-based conflicts. At the conclusion of the course, the student will 
understand the basic dynamics of conflict, most significant interventions used to manage 
conflict, benefits and costs of conflict, recognize his or her preferred style of conflict 
management and develop an understanding and appreciation of the conflict management styles 
of others.

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Computer Mediated Communication - Definitions and overview; Evolution of Computer Mediated Communication; 
Components of Computer Mediated Communication; Computer Mediated Discourse Analysis - Theories and faceted 
Approach; Information -Interactivity Dynamism in Computer Mediated Communication; Gender perspectives in 
Computer Mediated Communication; Privacy Issues in Computer Mediated Communication; Socialization in Social 
Media-Profiles, Identity and traversal; Computer Mediated Communication and technology acceptance; Computer 
Mediated Communication Theories; Human-Computer Interfaces. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
 
The objective of the course is to acquaint students with the practical and theoretical issues associated with computer - 
mediated communication (CMC) systems. The focus of the course will be on CMC and its influence on society as a 
mode of communication.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
Copywriting is the corner stone of ALL successful marketing. Copywriting empowers you with the ability to  
turn words into dollars.  Effective copy can play an important role in shaping perceptions about products, 
services and brands. The course requires a sound knowledge of advertising communications and will explore 
all aspects of writing for print, radio, television and online. It extensively prepares the students to write and 
develop ad copy for various media while selecting tone(s), style(s) and approach(es) for ad copy.…It further 
equips the students to communicate the strategy and specific assignments to a team using a Creative Brief.

services and brands. The course requires a sound knowledge of advertising communications and will explore 
all aspects of writing for print, radio, television and online. It extensively prepares the students to write and 
develop ad copy for various media while selecting tone(s), style(s) and approach(es) for ad copy.…It further 
equips the students to communicate the strategy and specific assignments to a team using a Creative Brief.

2. Scope and Objective of the course: 
 
The objective of the course is to acquaint students with the nature and functioning of language and the role it plays in 
the society. The fundamental linguistic concepts will be exemplified through English. Reference to Indian languages 
will also be made whenever possible.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description 
Introductory Lecture, Interpretation of Melody and Rhythm, Tonal Sequences, Musical scales, Elements 
of Raga and Taal, Naad, Musical Compositions, Forms and styles, Practical Application of Taals with 
various musical forms & styles of Hidustani and Carnatic music, Gharana system, Musical Instruments. 
 
2. Scope and objective of the course: 
Scope and objective of the course is to make the students aware of Raag and Taal System musical forms, 
and understanding the importance of Taal and Swargyan, style, techniques embellishments, aesthetical 
aspects of Indian Music etc. will be exposed through tapes and live performances. Carnatic music will 
also be touched upon, referring the Ragas common to Hindustani and Carnatic music.

interactive learning and real-world simulations.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: This course is floated to provide a brief understanding of how humans behave the way they 
do in an organization. This will be a highly informative course for people who want to understand the psychology of 
organizations and gain an in-depth understanding of the management functions of an organization at an individual level. 
The course would be highly relevant and suitable for students who wish to pursue a master’s in business schools because 
it will give them a sound theoretical understanding. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  To develop a conceptual framework for understanding organizations and 
their various functions from a psychological viewpoint. The course would help students understand the behavior of 
humans at different levels of hierarchy in an organization and the relevant issues and processes imbuing them.   
3. Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs): 
a) Students will know about what happens after they join the world of work. 
b) Students get to know what all operates and how to tackle various issues at workplace. 
c) Students will get first hand practical information related to adjusting in their respective workplaces.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Key concepts and histories of science fiction; major theoretical frameworks in SF; utopias, 
dystopias, and speculative futures; science fiction in relation to technological and ecological change; feminist, 
postcolonial, and global interventions in SF; engagements with artificial intelligence, posthumanism, and the animal; 
and the reimagining of cultural and ecological futures through speculative storytelling. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  
i) Introduce students to science fiction as a literary mode that critiques technological and social change. 
ii) Explore how science fiction engages with questions of environment and the posthuman through 
narrative. 
iii) Examine connections between science, technology, and ethics through speculative imagination. 
iv) Develop interdisciplinary skills by linking literary analysis with perspectives from history of 
science and cultural studies.

narrative. 
iii) Examine connections between science, technology, and ethics through speculative imagination. 
iv) Develop interdisciplinary skills by linking literary analysis with perspectives from history of 
science and cultural studies.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: This course is floated to provide a brief understanding of the practical ramification (or better 
subfield) of human resource management and deals with the significant issues related to developing human resources 
with special reference to its tripartite foundations of human betterment, organizational enhancement , and societal 
development. The course will help clarify the subtle difference between HR Management & HR Development. This will 
also enable curious minds to learn more about how training programs are planned, conceived, constructed, and delivered 
to potential stakeholders. HRD focuses on this core idea as to how the capabilities and credentials (and ultimately 
productivity) of the employees can be enhanced. 
2. Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs):  
a) To develop a conceptual framework for understanding human behavior in organizations and develop human capital 
(manpower) in various sectors and spheres of the world of work.  
b) The course would be very beneficial for students trying to understand the management functions of one very 
significant department of any organization. 
c) To get a superficial idea about various training/skill development exercises and processes encompassing such 
activities.

sources.text:
1. Course Description 
Preliminary Lecture, Logic and Science working behind music, Interval of Frequencies and interval of time, 
Scales- Hindustani, Carnatic and Western, Musical Streams, Notation Systemes, Principles of Thaat, Raga 
and Taal, Multiple speeds (Layakari), Philosophy and Psychology of music, Aesthetics of music, Voice 
Culture. 
2. Scope and objective of the course: 
The course aims to acquaint the students with the how and why of Music. It introduces the concepts of 
Musicology, Applied Theory, Rasa-Bhava and the working of Raga, Acoustics, some aspects of 
the textual and contextual development of music, the semantics of music, influence of music over mind 
and body, composers and compositions.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
This course introduces students the timeless wisdom spoken by Lord Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita 
and enables them to appreciate and apply those in daily life. Beginning with the fundamentals of the 
need to understand spirituality, the content includes science of soul, various types of yogic practices, 
viz., karma-yoga (action in God consciousness), jnana-yoga (philosophical research for truth), 
dhyana-yoga (meditative practice), astanga-yoga (eightfold yoga system) and culminates with bhakti-
yoga (devotional service to God). Adopting a topical approach, the course also touches upon t hese 
subject matters: the most confidential knowledge, three modes of material nature, nature, enjoyer and 
the consciousness, divine and demoniac qualities, and the perfection of knowledge.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
 Introduction-A survey of the international politics since the 20th century; Rise of Nationalism; 
World Wars, Emergence of IR as a discipline and the nature of its subject matter. 
 Key Defining Events in IR: Creation of United Nations, Cold War, Fall of USSR, September 11, 
China’s entry into WTO. 
 Key theoretical frameworks: Classical IR thinkers and their location within the existing IR canon 
that include realism, liberalism, constructivism, critical theory, and Asian theory of IR. 
 Key Agents of IR: State, Empire, International and sub-national agents, foreignpolicy. 
 Key Structures in IR: State-system, Eurocentrism, Post-colonialism, Globalization, Security and 
Global Governance 
 Key Institutions in IR: International Society, International Diplomacy, Great Powers, Balance of 
Power, War, International Law and Human Rights Regime and the Climate Change Regime. 
 Assorted Themes: Global Health Regime- Pandemic and IR 
 India’s Foreign Policy: Locating India’s space in the contemporary global order: identifying the 
opportunities and Challenges (India -Pakistan-China), India and China in South Asia; India and 
United States. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
International Relations is the study of an international system that is constituted by territorial states 
who enjoy sovereignty over matters of vital interests to them. This course offers the history of the 
international system, its functioning, theoretical frameworks, and the nature of the changing relations 
between the states and non -state actors. This course offers a critical reflection and analytical 
understanding of key defining events and the topical issues th at not only shaped but also confronted 
the existing international order. The course encourages students to engage in debates on the nature of 
international order as well as the responses to the challenges of the current international order. The 
course is designed to offer both the theoretical frameworks and critical reflections on the contemporary 
affairs. Moreover, the students will be able to make a clear perception of the relationship between the 
international relations as a discipline and the practice of world politics. Considerable sessions are 
devoted to understanding India’s role in the contemporary world too.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Ecocriticism has found its place in the Indian academy only in the last twenty years 
or so. The course is intended to  familiarize the learners with ecological, deep ecological and tinai critical 
principles and show them how these could be effective critical tools. The course gives a humanistic perspective 
on how ecology is a new paradigm in cultural and literary texts . The learners  will be exposed to recent 
ecocritical concepts which will challenge conventional attitudes and values which are detrimental to the well-
being of our planet. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  
1. To introduce the learners to one of the major postmodern critical trends. 
2. To familiarize the learners with some key ecocritical concepts. 
3. To equip the students to create ecocritical documents in literary, cinematic and other artistic forms. 
4. To train the learners in the application of the critical concepts to various cultural texts.

Course Description: 
AI-supported, process-oriented, portfolio-intensive academic writing practice; AI-assisted 
drafting support, editing and feedback evaluation with emphasis on originality and 
academic integrity; writing process stages including planning, drafting, feedback, revision 
and reflection; structured writing portfolio with drafts, feedback and revision evidence;  idea 
generation with a focus on clarity of thought; paragraph construction with topic sentences; 
logical sequencing and paragraph linking; organizational patterns including cause–effect, 
comparison, problem–solution and process description; text interpretation and 
transformation through summarizing, paraphrasing and originality maintenance; academic 
vocabulary; genre-based writing: analytical paragraphs, short essays, reflective responses, 
structured reports, data commentaries and case studies; visual information integration into 
writing; revision strategies for accuracy improvement; disciplinary and real-world 
contextualization of writing; reflective writing practices.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1.  Course Description:  
Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel 
operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion; 
Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations, 
classification. D.C generators, per formance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed 
control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic 
field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time 
harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase ind uction motors - classification and 
equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors; 
equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation. 
Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and 
speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.    
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt 
power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating character istics of 
Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this 
course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical -magnetic devices such as Transformer, 
DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed exper imental component for better 
understanding of the concepts.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1.  Course Description:  
Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel 
operation. Three phase transformer connections; Harmonic in transformers; Testing; Phase conversion; 
Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations, 
classification. D.C generators, per formance characteristics; D.C motors - torque/speed characteristics, speed 
control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic 
field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time 
harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase ind uction motors - classification and 
equivalent circuit. Synchronous machines: Constructional features; synchronous generators and motors; 
equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation. 
Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and 
speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.    
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt 
power applications. The scope of this course is to study of working principle & operating character istics of 
Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this 
course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical -magnetic devices such as Transformer, 
DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed exper imental component for better 
understanding of the concepts.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
An introduction to measurement techniques and instr umentation design and operation, the basic concept of units, 
measurement error and accuracy, Instrument design aspects, techniques and specifications of electronic instruments, the 
construction and design of measuring devices and measuring instruments such as Analog/ Digital meters, DSO, signal 
generators, signal analyzers, data loggers and recorders, electronic counters with their proper applications, Industrial 
Communication techniques, safety methods and instrumentation in hazardous areas.  The course will also consist of  
laboratory practice and lab assignments.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
 
This course introduces students to the principles and practical aspects of designing integrated circuits using 
CMOS technology. It covers both analog and digital VLSI design methodologies, exploring circuit -level 
building blocks, layout considerations, and performance trade-offs. Emphasis is placed on low-power, area-
efficient, and high -performance circuit techniques, along with exp osure to modern CAD tools and 
fabrication-aware design strategies. Students will gain experience designing critical components, including 
logic gates, adders, amplifiers, and mixed-signal interfaces.

 Quick review of Vector Spaces and Linear Transformations, Basis and Dimension, 
 rank-nullity theorem, change of basis; Inner product spaces, Cauchy Schwarz's 
 inequality, GramSchmidt orthonormalization, QR decomposition, Discrete Fourier 
 Transform, and their applications, Spectral Theorem, Cayley-Hamilton Theorem, 
 Decomposition theorem, and Jordan canonical forms, applications of SVD in 
 Principal Component Analysis, use of SVD in low-rank approximations and to find 
 least-squares solutions.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description  
Object orientation concepts, theories and principles; fundamental concepts of the object mod el: classes, objects, 
methods and messages, encapsulation and inheritance, interface and implementation, reuse and extension of 
classes, inheritance and polymorphism; overloading and overriding; static and dynamic binding; multithreaded 
programming; event handling and exception handling; process of object oriented requirements specification, 
analysis and design; notations for object -oriented analysis and design; case studies and applications using some 
object oriented programming languages. Object Oriented Design Patterns: Behavioural, Structural and 
Creational. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course 
a) Gives an in-depth understanding of object-oriented programming using the java programming language, object-
oriented analysis and design, and design patterns.  
b) In the classroom, the course will be taught with live demonstrations, running and debugging several examples on 
tools like Eclipse.  
c) The latter part of the course focuses on designing object-oriented software.  
 
3. Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs) 
On successful completion of this course, students will be able to: 
CLO1. Explain the principles of object-oriented programming and apply core concepts such as abstraction, 
encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism in software development. 
CLO2. Design, implement, test, and debug medium-sized Java programs using classes, objects, interfaces, 
collections, generics, exception handling, file I/O, and multithreading. 
CLO3. Analyse object-oriented software requirements and represent software designs using appropriate 
UML diagrams and object-oriented design principles. 
CLO4. Apply commonly used object-oriented design patterns to develop software that is modular, reusable, 
extensible, and maintainable. 
CLO5. Evaluate alternative object-oriented design and implementation choices based on software quality 
attributes such as maintainability, flexibility, and reusability.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:
Set theory: Sets, relations and functions, equivalence relations, partially ordered sets, countability of sets,
lattices and Boolean algebras;
Logic and methods of proof: Propositional logic, language of propositional logic, predicate logic and logical
inference with quantifiers, introduction to different standard proof techniques;
Combinatorics: Counting techniques, pigeonhole principle, inclusion-exclusion principle, recurrence relations,
generating function, partitions;
Graph theory: Graphs and digraphs, special types of graphs, trees, isomorphism, connectedness, Euler and
Hamilton graphs.
2. Scope & Objective of the Course:
Mathematics, described as a language of science, has acquired its unique position due to its precision and
rigour. This makes essential the development of the sense for mathematical rigor as well as the habit of math-
ematical thought process. The course will achieve this by introducing students to propositional and predicate
logic. As an important follow-up, various methods of proof will be discussed. Several mathematical struc-
tures like relations and orderings are studied due to their importance, not only in mathematics but also applied
subjects like computer science. The course is also useful for the preparation for the study of computational
concepts, techniques, and skills necessary to comprehend the structure of problems encountered in the design
and analysis of algorithms.

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: Groups, subgroups, a counting principle, normal subgroups, and quotient 
groups, Cayley’s theorem, automorphisms, permutation groups, Sylow’s theorems, Rings, ring of 
real quaternions, ideals and quotient rings, homomorphisms, Euclidean rings, polynomial rings, and 
polynomials over the rational field. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:   
  
The objective of this course is to provide an introduction to abstract algebraic structures, including 
groups and rings. The abstract setting allows for the study of disparate mathematical objects together. 
We can derive properties and structures that apply to concrete examples. We will see examples from 
number theory, linear algebra and geometry.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
Course Description: This course introduces the mathematical foundations of data science with emphasis 
on probability, Gaussian models, statistical inference, nonparametric methods, optimization, 
dimensionality reduction, data preparation, and scalable data analytics. It develops core tools such as 
probability bounds, Bayesian inference, PCA and SVD, kernel density estimation, nearest-neighbor 
methods, and connects them to practical data-analysis problems. 
Pre-requisites: The course is self-contained. However, a basic understanding of probability theory, 
calculus, linear algebra, and elementary programming would be helpful.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Mathematical Modeling in Biology, Epidemiology, Model for Various Problems and 
Situation Using ODE and PDE, Classic Models in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, Equilibria and Stability 
Analysis, Dynamics of Class-Structured Populations, Techniques for Analyzing Models. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: The principal objective of this course is to familiarize students with 
the theory of population and a basic understanding of mathematical modelling of a real-world problem. 
Students will gain enough background to read theoretical population and evolutionary ecology literature, do 
simple modelling, and springboard to more complex theory if desired. Students will develop techniques for 
understanding and analysing simple, multivariate, and nonlinear models will be explored.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which 
are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and 
geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation 
and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus 
introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts 
play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and 
numerous other applications. 
The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real -world phenomena such as 
motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series, 
power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives,  and vector calculus, leading to 
fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss. 
 
2. Scope and objectives of the course: 
 To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables. 
 Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization. 
 To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass. 
 Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields. 
 To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses.

1. Course Description 
This course presents the study of differential equations with the objective of introducing the 
classical methods for solving boundary value problems. It also serves as a basis for the applications 
of differential equations, Fourier series and Laplace trans form in the various branches of 
engineering and sciences. Furthermore, it emphasizes on the role of orthogonal polynomials in 
dealing with Sturm-Liouville problems.

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: Introduction to op timization; linear programming; simplex methods; duality 
and sensitivity analysis; transportation model and its variants; integer linear programming 
nonlinear programming; multi-objective optimization; evolutionary computation techniques. 
 
2. Scope and Object ive: Engineers, scientists, analysts, and managers often face the challenge of 
making trade -offs between different factors to achieve desirable outcomes. Optimization is the 
process of making these trade-offs in the best possible way. Over the years, optimization problems 
have become well -established and are encountered in the physical sciences, engineering, 
economics, industry, planning, and many other areas of human activity. The objective of this course 
is to familiarize students with standard methods of solving optimization problems. 
This course covers various aspects of optimization, including a description of techniques such as 
Linear Programming and Nonlinear Programming, and their applications in various engineering and 
science disciplines, including economics and finance. Multi-objective optimization, which addresses 
optimization with more than one objective, is also discussed. Additionally, the course provides a 
brief and informative overview of the non- traditional optimization technique, Genetic Algorithms.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:
Set theory: Sets, relations and functions, equivalence relations, partially ordered sets, countability of sets,
lattices and Boolean algebras;
Logic and methods of proof: Propositional logic, language of propositional logic, predicate logic and logical
inference with quantifiers, introduction to different standard proof techniques;
Combinatorics: Counting techniques, pigeonhole principle, inclusion-exclusion principle, recurrence relations,
generating function, partitions;
Graph theory: Graphs and digraphs, special types of graphs, trees, isomorphism, connectedness, Euler and
Hamilton graphs.
2. Scope & Objective of the Course:
Mathematics, described as a language of science, has acquired its unique position due to its precision and
rigour. This makes essential the development of the sense for mathematical rigor as well as the habit of math-
ematical thought process. The course will achieve this by introducing students to propositional and predicate
logic. As an important follow-up, various methods of proof will be discussed. Several mathematical struc-
tures like relations and orderings are studied due to their importance, not only in mathematics but also applied
subjects like computer science. The course is also useful for the preparation for the study of computational
concepts, techniques, and skills necessary to comprehend the structure of problems encountered in the design
and analysis of algorithms.

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: Groups, subgroups, a counting principle, normal subgroups, and quotient 
groups, Cayley’s theorem, automorphisms, permutation groups, Sylow’s theorems, Rings, ring of 
real quaternions, ideals and quotient rings, homomorphisms, Euclidean rings, polynomial rings, and 
polynomials over the rational field. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:   
  
The objective of this course is to provide an introduction to abstract algebraic structures, including 
groups and rings. The abstract setting allows for the study of disparate mathematical objects together. 
We can derive properties and structures that apply to concrete examples. We will see examples from 
number theory, linear algebra and geometry.

    Solution of non-linear algebraic equations; interpolation and approximation; numerical

the error analysis of different algorithms.

syllabus.heading: COURSE DESCRIPTION

sources.text:
COURSE DESCRIPTION:  Combinatorics is often described briefly as being about counting, and indeed 
counting is a large part of combinatorics.  As the name suggests, however, it is broader than this: it is about 
combining things. Questions that arise include counting problems:  
“How many ways can these elements be combined?”  
But there are other questions, such as whether a certain combination is possible, or what combination is the 
“best” in some sense. 
This course presents the different methods to solve the counting problems . We will mainly focus on 
combinatorial approach instead of algebraic approach.

sources.text:
Instructor   :  Sumanta Pasari 
 
1. Course Desccription: 
This course on Time Series Analysis and Forecasting covers introductory concepts of trend, seasonality, 
and cyclicity in time series data. It r eviews extrapolative and decomposition models and smoothing 
techniques. Discussions include autoregressive error structure – auto-covariance and auto-correlation, ACF, 
and PACF.  Linear stationary model analysis, such as AR, MA, ARMA  is included along with e rror 
diagnostics. It includes Box-Jenkins time series analysis and linear non-stationary models, such as ARIMA, 
SARIMA, and ARFIMA. Finally, we study some models with stochastic variance – ARCH and GARCH. 
The cou rse includes discussions  on m ultivariate time series models and associated techniques. It  
necessarily involves the use of statistical software and programming languages for hands-on practice. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This 4th level course introduces time series analysis and associated forecasting techniques, in which students 
will be equipped with various forecasting techniques and knowledge on modern statistical methods for 
analyzing time series data. The course reviews extrapolative and decomposition m odels, introduction to 
Box–Jenkins time series analysis, and ARIMA m odels.  The remainder of the course considers various 
practical aspects of the principles behind modern forecasting techniq ues. Students will study and develop 
the ability to select appropriate model to carry out forecasting. A one-hour lab will be conducted every 
week. Students will learn how to explore and analyze different types of time s eries data using R  
programming.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1.   Course Description:  
Applied Statistics is an exciting sub-area of Statistics. It has application in almost all science disciplines 
which deal with data and uncertainty. This course builds up fundamental concepts of various key statis-
tical methods necessary to analyze/interpret a variety of practical business/engineering problems. This 
course emphasizes the role of statistics in one’s own field of study by making sense of data, developing 
self-ability to apply appropriate statistical methods, performing experimental designs and above all, re-
alizing the limitations/inherent assumptions in a statistical test to avoid over interpretation or misinter-
pretation. The thrust areas covered in this course include probability distributions, statistical inference, 
analysis of variance (ANOVA), regression and correlation, discriminant analysis, factor and cluster 
analysis, time series analysis and forecasting, nonparametric methods and statistical quality control. The 
theoretical learning will be complemented with various case studies and hands-on training in excel/R. 
2.   Scope and objective of the course: 
This 4 th level course is designed with a two -fold purpose. First, it will provide an exposure to various  
theoretical univariate/multivariate methods and their practical applications. Second , this course will 
improve methodological/analytical maturity to attempt a variety of problems using MS-excel and R.

1. Course Description:  
This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which 
are essential tools in enginee ring and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and 
geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation 
and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus 
introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts 
play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and 
numerous other applications. 
The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real -world phenomena such as 
motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series, 
power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives,  and vector calculus, leading to 
fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss. 
 
2. Scope and objectives of the course: 
 To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables. 
 Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization. 
 To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass. 
 Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields. 
 To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses.

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: Review of coordinate geometry, Rational Fractions, Complex Numbers and quadratic 
equations, Matrices and determinants, Progression and series, permutations and combinations, Binomial 
theorem, Functions: Polynomial, Trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic etc., One variable Calculus: Limit and 
continuity, Differentiation, Integration. Applications of derivatives and definite integration. Program-specific 
applications of the above mathematical concepts. 
2. Scopes and objective of the course:   
This Course deals with intermediate mathematics that is essential  for PCB students who joined BE (E&S 
engineering).   Course covers set theory, Functions, Coordinate geometry, basic algebra & theory of equations, 
permutations and combinations, Binomial theorem, Trigonometry, One Dimensional Calculus: Limit and 
continuity, Differentiation, Integration, Application of derivatives and definite integration.

attendance.heading: Attendance Policy

sources.text:
Attendance Policy: Each student is expected to attend all classes, tutorials, and practical sessions and 
to participate in all evaluation components. A 10% weight is assigned to assessment linked to 
attendance and participation. To this end, a small surprise quiz will be con ducted in the tutorial class. 
The scores in surprise quizzes linked to attendance and participation will be considered in the final 
score. This score will be considered only for students with a minimum attendance of 50% in the 
lecture and tutorial classes separately. For students with attendance less than 50% in either the 
lecture or tutorial class, zero marks will be assigned, irrespective of the scores in the surprise quizzes 
attempted.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:
This course covers the following topics: Mathematical preliminaries; Fluid statics and forces on
submerged bodies; Integral relations for a control volume; Mass, Momentum and Energy Con-
servation; Reynolds Transport Theorem; Differential relations for fluid flow, Analytical solution of
Navier-Stokes equation; Dimensional analysis and similarity; Inviscid potential flows; Bernoulli’s
Equation; Internal and external viscous flows; Basic compressible flows.
2. Scope & Objectives of the Course:
The objectives of the course are to learn about the following topics:
• Introduction to fluid mechanics and establish its relevance in mechanical engineering.
• Derivation of the equations governing mass, momentum and energy transport.
• Application of the governing equation to solve simple fluid mechanics problems.
• Non-dimensionalization of governing equations and identification of dimensionless 
numbers, Modeling and similarity concepts.
• Two dimensional, inviscid, potential flows; Stream function, Velocity potential.
• Analyze laminar and turbulent flows inside pipes, External flow past immersed bodies, 
Intro- duction to Boundary layer theory
• One dimensional, compressible flow inside ducts of variable cross-section, normal and 
oblique shocks.
