sources.text:
Instructor-in-Charge     :  Aniruddha Roy 
 
1. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
      This course covers key immunologic concepts: how the components of the immune system are generated, 
organized, and function; the mechanisms that lead to beneficial immune responses, immune disorders, and 
immunodeficiencies; methods to identify immune react ions; and ways to manipulate the immune system and its 
components to benefit the patient. This course will give the students an advanced understanding of the principles and 
mechanisms of the immune system and immune responses in the context of infection, malignancy and immunological 
disorders. The course will also enable the students to describe the fundamental mechanisms underlying immunologic 
disease and associate these mechanisms with strategies for therapeutic modulation of the immune system. It will help 
the students to gain the necessary transferable and research skills in basic and clinical immunology to promote lifelong 
learning and career development.

Course Title  :  Modern Pharmaceutical Analytical Techniques

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
This course is a labora tory oriented course and covers  various analytical aspects like  principles of sample 
preparation, method development for analysis and characterization of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API) 
and formulations,  using techniques such as High Performance Liquid chromatography (HPLC), bio -
chromatography, size exclusion, affinity, chiral, fast protein  liquid chromatography (FPLC). Characterization of 
nanopharmaceutcials using Atomic Force Microscopy  (AFM), Scanning Electron Microscopy  (SEM), 
Transmission Electron Microscopy  (TEM), Dynamic Light Scattering  (DLS) techniques. 1H and 13C Nuclear 
Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy in structural characterization, Mass Spectrometry and its applications, 
Elemental analysis, Optical, chiro-optical techniques in structure elucidation. 
 
2. Scope of the Course: 
The course is aimed at exposing the students to modern analytical techniques in relevance to pharmaceutical 
industries. Traini ng with respect to the handling and operation of sophisticated instruments, interpretation of 
results obtained for the characterization of molecules, their qualitative and quantitative evaluation are emphasized. 
Objectives of the Course: 
Exposure to principles, instrumentation, calibration and operation of analytical instruments. 
Obtaining spectral data, their interpretation, evaluation of qualitative and quantitative  aspects of drugs and their 
estimation.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
 
Physicochemical principles involved in effective formulation development, including various aspects like, 
pharmaceutical preformulation including bulk characteristics, polymorphism, solubility analysis, solid and 
solution state stability, compatibility. This course also cover various ICH guidelines like stability study, 
specifications, impurities which are required during formulation development. This course also discussed 
details about mechanical properties of powders, principles of dissolution, in -vitro in -vivo correlation 
(IVIVC), polymer science, etc. 
2. Scope and objective of the course: 
 
Prior to the deve lopment of any dosage form with a new or old drug candidate, it is essential that certain 
fundamental physical and chemical properties of the drug molecule and other derived properties of the drug 
are determined. This information dictates possible approaches in formulation development. The aim of this 
course is to make the students understand those physicochemical principles which must be applied in the 
formulation and development of an efficacious dosage form, so that required duration and intensity of effect 
can be ensured at the intended site of action. 
3. Text Book (TB): 
 
TB 1: Carstensen, J. T, Pharmaceutical Preformulation. Technomic Publishing comp. USA. 
 
4. Reference Books (R): R1: Carstensen, J. T., Rhodes, C.T., 2000. Drug Stability: Principles and Practices, 
Drugs and Pharm. Sci. Series, Vol. 43, 3rd edn, Marcel Dekker Inc., New York.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
Overview of new drug research and development; Bioethics and institutional review board; 
regulatory control of clinical trials for NDA & ANDA application; Good Clinical Practice (GCP); 
related ICH guidelines; applied clinical epidemiology and biostatistics; clinical trial study 
design; trial development (protocol, case report form , and data management); clinical trial 
management- coordinating clinical trial at the site, documentation methodology, 
implementing monitoring plan and performing quality control; statistical analysis and data 
interpretation; monitoring obligations and methods; and Medical writing & report 
preparation for various submissions.  
2. Scope and Objective of the course: 
There is a growing need for clinical researchers in the health industries (pharmaceutical, 
biotechnology/medical device companies, research institutes, and hospitals) involved in the 
development of new drugs and therapies. This course is aimed at training students in 
conducting clinical trials on humans with new drugs/therapies before they are introduced to 
the market. Students completing the coursework will gain specialized knowledge and skills 
required to design, monitor , and manage clinical trials. Cours es include the drug 
development process; regulations, guidelines , and standards; research methodology and 
biostatistics; clinical trial organization, monitoring , and documentation; and project 
management.  
3. Text Book (T): 
T1: Lawrence M Friedman, Curt D Furberg  and David L DeMets, "Fundamentals of 
Clinical Trials”, Spring Verlag, New York, 5th Ed., 2015. 
T2: Shein-Chung Chow, Jen -Pei Liu, “Design and Analysis of C linical Trials”, Wiley -IEEE, 
2013.  
Reference Books (R): 
R1: Steven Piantadosi, “Clinical Trials -A Methodologic Perspective”, John Wiley & Sons, 
2005. 
R2: R A Guarino, "New Drug Approval Process" Marcel Dekker, New York, 2 nd Edn., Vol. 56, 
1993.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
Introduction to pharmacokinetic modeling of drugs; Compartmental modeling including one 
compartmental and two compartmental models; Non-compartmental analysis (NCA); Bioequivalence and 
comparative bioavailability studies; Pharmacokinetic Pharmacodynamic modeling techniques, 
determination of order of absorption and absorption rate constant by Wagner-Nelson method; non-linear 
pharmacokinetics; Pharmacokinetic drug interactions; multi-dose pharmacokinetics of drugs following one 
compartmental model; Design of multi-dose regimen; Dosage regimen adjustment in renal impairment; 
Application of the pharmacokinetic principles for better therapeutic outcomes 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
The course imparts knowledge of pharmacokinetics, its application, pharmacokinetic studies, mathematical 
modeling, and experimental design. This will help students to gain knowledge in a very important area of 
pharmacy. Practicals are designed to expose students to pharmacokinetic studies.

sources.text:
Instructors     
 
Scope and objective of the course:  
The course deals with the principles and techniques of biotechnology with direct application in the 
field of pharmaceutical sciences. It aims at bringing together the principles of molecular bio logy, 
molecular genetics, biochemical engineering, protein engineering, enzymtechnology, bio -
informatics required to develop a successful biotechnology based pharmaceutical product. The 
applications of genetic engineering, recombinant DNA technology, hybri doma technology, 
transgenic animals, gene therapy, drug delivery aspects of biotechnology products and their clinical 
evaluation are also dealt with in this course.    
 
1. Text Book (TB):  
Bernard R. Glick, Jack J. Pasternak, Molecular Biotechnology- Principles and Apllication of  rDNA. 
2nd edition, ASM Press, Washington, 1998. 
2. Reference Books (R):  
R1: Brown T. A., Gene Cloning & DNA Analysis An Introduction 6th edition. Blackwell Publishing, 
UK, 2010. 
R2: Balasubramanian D., Bryce, C.F.A., Dharmalingam, K., Green, J., Jayaraman, K. Concepts in 
Biotechnology, urvey University Press, Hyderabad, India, 1996. 
 
 
 
: Dr. Gautam Kumar

sources.text:
Instructors     
 
Scope and objective of the course:  
The course deals with the principles and techniques of biotechnology with direct application in the 
field of pharmaceutical sciences. It aims at bringing together the principles of molecular bio logy, 
molecular genetics, biochemical engineering, protein engineering, enzymtechnology, bio -
informatics required to develop a successful biotechnology based pharmaceutical product. The 
applications of genetic engineering, recombinant DNA technology, hybri doma technology, 
transgenic animals, gene therapy, drug delivery aspects of biotechnology products and their clinical 
evaluation are also dealt with in this course.    
 
1. Text Book (TB):  
Bernard R. Glick, Jack J. Pasternak, Molecular Biotechnology- Principles and Apllication of  rDNA. 
2nd edition, ASM Press, Washington, 1998. 
2. Reference Books (R):  
R1: Brown T. A., Gene Cloning & DNA Analysis An Introduction 6th edition. Blackwell Publishing, 
UK, 2010. 
R2: Balasubramanian D., Bryce, C.F.A., Dharmalingam, K., Green, J., Jayaraman, K. Concepts in 
Biotechnology, urvey University Press, Hyderabad, India, 1996. 
 
 
 
: Dr. Gautam Kumar

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: This course introduces students to various organizational aspects, focusing on pharmaceutical 
management. Topics include technology innovation, drug planning, strategy, project execution, product 
development, production, scale-up, marketing, IPR, HR, industrial relations, documentation, R&D, and ethics. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  The objective of the course is to help students understand new drug and 
product considerations and planning ; strategic considerations; project implementation; product development; 
production management & scale-up; marketing strategy; human resources development; ethical issues;  and R&D 
management.

instructor in -charge will be announced in the class and shall be based on the

All evaluation components are equally important, irrespective of weightage. Hence, students failing to attend 
scheduled classes, or absenting themselves in one or many of the evaluation components, may become  
ineligible for obtaining a valid grade at the en d of the semester. Attendance in lectures and practicals are all

examinations**, and in practical (laboratory) components, se parately ( i.e. procuring low marks in 
evaluation components, aforementioned**, other than laboratory practicals, would not suffice, to clear 
the course).

Course Title : Advanced Drug Delivery Systems

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
A study of physicochemical and biopharmaceutical factors involved in the design of novel drug delivery systems like 
mucosal, particulate systems for systemic delivery of bioactive molecules. Special considerations for delivery of protein, 
peptide and other biological products. In vitro and in vivo evaluation of novel drug delivery systems 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
The prime objective of this course is to impart knowledge of design, development and evaluation of novel drug delivery 
systems (NDDS). The primary focus would be on integrating the biopharmaceutical, physiochemical and physiological 
properties for design and development of (NDDS) with due consideration of pharmacological action. Excipients used 
in design and development of NDDS would be covered exhaustively.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: This course deals with the strategy and tactics involved in the synthesis of organic 
molecules. The idea is to identify key structural features in the target molecules and then go backward logically 
to identify appropriate starting materials and chemical reactions  for their synthesis. Knowledge and 
understanding of common organic reagents and reaction mechanisms are required for this course. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  Most life-saving drugs are organic molecules. This course aims to 
develop a logical understanding which can be used to propose the synthesis of an organic compound. This 
course teaches various strategies and tactics together with the common nomenclature used in Retrosynthetic 
Analysis. At the end of the course , students should be able to propose a synthetic scheme for various drug 
molecules with appropriate justification.

sources.text:
Team of Instructors : Jagdish Chand, Talati Yugant Krishna, Jyoti Verma 
 
1. Scope and Objective of the Course : 
 
The objective of this course is to understand the principles of experimental pharmacology with 
special emphasis on in-vitro cell culture techniques and in vivo experimentation. Basics of animal 
handling, breeding, diet manipulation, dose Calculation-Human equivalent dose, development of 
new animal models and evaluation techniques for various diseases and their standardization will be 
covered. The course also includes toxicological, teratogenic, carcinogenic studies, and data analysis 
 
2. Text Books ( TB ): 
 
N. S. Parmar, Shiv Prakash, “Screening Methods in Pharmacology”- Alpha Science International, 
2006 , Reprint 2011-Narosa publications 
 
 
3. Reference Books ( RB ): 
 
1. H Gerhard Vogel, “ Drug Discovery and Evaluation- Pharmacological Assays” – II 
Edition, Springer, 2002 
 
2.Laurence L Brunton, “Goodman and Gilman’s Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics”- 
XII Edition, Mc-Graw Hill, New York, 2011

sources.text:
Team of Instructors : Jagdish Chand, Talati Yugant Krishna, Jyoti Verma 
 
1. Scope and Objective of the Course : 
 
The objective of this course is to understand the principles of experimental pharmacology with 
special emphasis on in-vitro cell culture techniques and in vivo experimentation. Basics of animal 
handling, breeding, diet manipulation, dose Calculation-Human equivalent dose, development of 
new animal models and evaluation techniques for various diseases and their standardization will be 
covered. The course also includes toxicological, teratogenic, carcinogenic studies, and data analysis 
 
2. Text Books ( TB ): 
 
N. S. Parmar, Shiv Prakash, “Screening Methods in Pharmacology”- Alpha Science International, 
2006 , Reprint 2011-Narosa publications 
 
 
3. Reference Books ( RB ): 
 
1. H Gerhard Vogel, “ Drug Discovery and Evaluation- Pharmacological Assays” – II 
Edition, Springer, 2002 
 
2.Laurence L Brunton, “Goodman and Gilman’s Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics”- 
XII Edition, Mc-Graw Hill, New York, 2011

Instructor-in-Charge     :  Aniruddha Roy 
 
1. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
      This course includes the analysis of polymers and biopolymers at a molecular scale, and design of devices used in 
contact with biological systems. Topics include molecular interactions between bio - and synthetic molecules and 
surfaces; design, synthesis, and processing approaches for materials that control cell functions; and application of 
state-of-the-art materials science to problems in tissue engineering, drug delivery, vaccines, and cell-guiding surfaces. 
This course covers the fundamental concep ts (physical chemistry, chemistry, and materials physics, and biology) 
behind the design at a molecular scale of synthetic materials with biological functions.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
The course will cover all aspects of  the rationale and purpose of preclinical toxicology studies of new drugs 
under development. It gives an in -depth understanding of the basic principles and mechanisms of 
toxicology, different classes of toxicants,  dose and the concept of  t h e  dose-response relationship, 
Toxicokinetics, and toxicodynamics, OECD guidelines for toxicological study,  International Council for 
Harmonization (ICH) guidelines, toxicity testing methods in organ systems. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: Students who have undergone the course are expected to 
a) Understand the molecular mechanisms of toxicity 
b) Understand the guidelines and methods of testing for toxicity studies 
c) Understand the regulatory requirements of preclinical toxicological studies 
d) Understand the ICH and OCED guidelines for preclinical toxicity testing and safety Pharmacology

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
The course will cover all aspects of  the rationale and purpose of preclinical toxicology studies of new drugs 
under development. It gives an in -depth understanding of the basic principles and mechanisms of 
toxicology, different classes of toxicants,  dose and the concept of  t h e  dose-response relationship, 
Toxicokinetics, and toxicodynamics, OECD guidelines for toxicological study,  International Council for 
Harmonization (ICH) guidelines, toxicity testing methods in organ systems. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: Students who have undergone the course are expected to 
a) Understand the molecular mechanisms of toxicity 
b) Understand the guidelines and methods of testing for toxicity studies 
c) Understand the regulatory requirements of preclinical toxicological studies 
d) Understand the ICH and OCED guidelines for preclinical toxicity testing and safety Pharmacology

syllabus.heading: Course description

sources.text:
1. Course description: Molecular pharmacology deals with understanding the molecular basis for 
the actions of drugs and the characteristics of interactions between drug molecules and those of 
the substrates of drug action in the cell. Course will include chemical, molecular biological and all 
biochemical and cell biological techniques to understand how cells respond to pharmacologic 
agents. 
2. Scope and objectives of the course: 
a) To impart advance knowledge about the epigenetic changes involved  in the disease  
development. 
b) To give advanced knowledge regarding the molecular mechanisms involved in the drug 
action.

Course Description: This course introduces the principles of classical mechanics from Newtonian and analytical  
perspectives. It covers constrained motion, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations, variational principles,  
central-force dynamics, canonical transformations, Poisson brackets, the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies 
in inertial, and rotating reference frames.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Electromagnetic Theory I is the first of two courses in Electromagnetic Theory for 
Physics students and is also required for Chemistry students. This course covers topics in electricity, 
magnetism, and electromagnetic waves. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
 Learn the mathematical tools needed to solve problems in electromagnetism 
 Understand the concept of electric field 
 Solve electrostatic problems using the concept of potential 
 Understand how electric field is modified in materials 
 Understand the concept of magnetic field 
 Understand how magnetic field is modified in materials 
 Learn about magnetic induction and the basics of electrodynamics 
 Introduction to Maxwell’s equations and electromagnetic waves

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: The course will cover Geometrical optics, wave optics, Diffraction, Laser theory, and the recent trends of 
research in the optical physics. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
The objective of the course is to give an introduction to basic phenomena in optics and the techniques used to deal with them . The recent 
development of the subject and its application in the research level will be discussed. Course will assume a basic kno wledge of optics at the 
level of the core Physics courses. The course will also provide theoretical background for the optics experiments done in Ele ctromagnetism & 
Optics Lab. (PHYF214).

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:         
This course is the second of the two-semesters course on Quantum Mechanics and is a continuation of Quantum 
Mechanics I. In this course we will discuss quantum theory of angular momentum and addition of angular 
momentum, applications to spherically symmetric potential, approximation methods to time independent systems, 
and time dependent systems.    
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
 
● Quantum theory of angular momentum.  
● Three-Dimensional Problems in Quantum Mechanics, Central Potential problem 
● Time independent approximation methods in quantum mechanics 
● Quantum mechanics of time-dependent systems and quantum theory of scattering.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
The course introduces elementary computational methods for obtaining approximate solutions to 
mathematical problems arising in physics. Topics include root finding, systems of linear equations, 
numerical quadrature, ordinary and partial differential equati ons, Monte Carlo simulation, and Markov 
Chain Monte Carlo methods. Emphasis will be placed on the hands -on implementation of basic 
algorithms and their application to representative physical systems. 
 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:  
The objective of the course is to develop a practical understanding of the basic numerical methods used 
to obtain approximate solutions of mathematical problems arising in physics. Emphasis will be placed on 
the hands -on construction of elementary algorithms, the translation of equations into finite 
computational procedures, and the interpretation and validation of numerical results. Students will also 
learn to use scientific  programming and visualization tools, including Monte Carlo and Markov Chain 
Monte Carlo techniques, for studying relevant physical systems.

1. Course Description: (Just as every book has a preface, I will avail this space to elaborate about the 
course in great detail. It will be a synopsis of particle physics , providing context for the questions it 
addresses and a sense of the answers that will be discussed in the course. Hopefully, it will give you a 
fair idea of  what particl e physics is all about and what to expect from this course.  The titles of 
paragraphs may seem out of place or even nonsensical in the first reading. Some things will fall in 
place as you read through the handout. For some other stuff, you may have to wait till the end of the 
course.) 
 
Bright blue sky:  
 
What are the most fundamental questions we can pose in Physics? 
1. What are the most fundamental building blocks (called particles for the want of a better word) of the 
Universe? 
2. What are the fundamental forces (interaction is a better word) that bind them to form the structural 
hierarchy we see at different levels? 
3. What can we know about the particles and their dynamics if we know the answers to the above 
questions? 
4. Are there fundamental principles that mandate the existence of different kinds of fundamental 
particles and different kinds of fundamental interactions? Is there an overarching theme in the 
answers we know? 
Particle Physics aims to offer concrete answers to the above questions, though some caveats remain. Our 
present understanding of these questions is summarised in the so-called Standard Model (SM) of Particle 
Physics. This course will offer some answers within the framework of the Standard Model of Particle 
Physics.  
 
Relativity + Quantum Mechanics = Quantum Field Theory:  
 
Before I give a glimpse of answers to the above questions, we must ask for the framework for particle 
physics. It turns out that the natural framework for particle physics is a quantum theory for a system of 
fields. Let us understand the reason behind this. We will be talking about the most fundamental particles and 
their interactions at the minutest length scales, so quantum mechanics is inescapable. To study smaller and 
smaller length scales, we need probes whose wavelengths are sufficiently small. Thus, we use extremely 
high-energy particles (relativistic velocities imply larger momentum and hence smaller wavelengths). 
Hence, special relativity is a must. How about the study of mesons (bound states of quarks-antiquarks) and

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:
Soft matter or soft condensed matter is a subfield of condensed matter comprising a variety of physical systems
that are deformed or structurally altered by thermal or mechanical stress of the magnitude of thermal fluctuations.
They include liquids, colloids, polymers, foams, gels, granular materials, liquid crystals, and biomolecules. These
materials share an essential characteristic feature in that predominant physical behaviors occur at an energy scale
comparable with room temperature thermal energy. At these temperatures, quantum aspects are less significant.
In this course, our aim would be to understand the structure, properties, and dynamics of the soft matter.
What is the order of forces and times scales that affect the overall behaviour of this class of matter?
2. Scope & Objective of the Course:
• Develop familiarity with the basics of soft condensed matter.
• To develop an understanding about the forces and order of thermal fluctuations in soft matter.
• Why some part of matter is classified as soft matter?

Course Title              :  Group Theory and Applications

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
This is an introductory course on Group Theory, designed for undergraduates and PhD scholars, with 
an emphasis on applications in physics. Many physical systems exhibit symmetry, which allows for a 
simplified analysis. The mathematical language of describing and studying a vast class of these 
symmetries is Group Theory.  In each case, the symmetry operations are represented by individual 
group elements and their combinations. Discrete symmetries entail discrete groups, which may contain 
a finite or infinite number of elements. Continuous symmetries entail continuous groups (also called as 
‘Lie groups’). In this course, we will cover the structure, classification, and representations of groups. 
We will see how group theory can help us understands some aspects of quantum mechanics, classical 
mechanics, and most importantly, particle interactions.  
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
•Identify and classify discrete and continuous symmetries in physical systems using the foundational 
concepts of group theory. 
•Apply the principles of representation theory to decompose group representations into irreducible 
components and interpret their physical significance. 
•Demonstrate the application of group theory in quantum mechanics by analyzing the symmetry 
structure of the hydrogen atom and explaining the role of conserved quantities and degeneracies. 
•Analyze physical systems under spacetime symmetry transformations using continuous groups such 
as the Lorentz and Poincaré groups. 
•Analyze particle interactions and fundamental forces using the mathematical framework of Lie 
groups and Lie algebras.

symmetries is Group Theory.  In each case, the symmetry operations are represented by individual 
group elements and their combinations. Discrete symmetries entail discrete groups, which may contain 
a finite or infinite number of elements. Continuous symmetries entail continuous groups (also called as 
‘Lie groups’). In this course, we will cover the structure, classification, and representations of groups. 
We will see how group theory can help us understands some aspects of quantum mechanics, classical 
mechanics, and most importantly, particle interactions.  
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
•Identify and classify discrete and continuous symmetries in physical systems using the foundational 
concepts of group theory. 
•Apply the principles of representation theory to decompose group representations into irreducible 
components and interpret their physical significance. 
•Demonstrate the application of group theory in quantum mechanics by analyzing the symmetry 
structure of the hydrogen atom and explaining the role of conserved quantities and degeneracies. 
•Analyze physical systems under spacetime symmetry transformations using continuous groups such 
as the Lorentz and Poincaré groups. 
•Analyze particle interactions and fundamental forces using the mathematical framework of Lie 
groups and Lie algebras.

Course Title: Physics of Semiconductor Devices

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
This course will discuss the physics behind the semiconductors and the devices. The structure of any solid material plays 
an important role in their operation; the discussion will start with basic crystal structures and will cover the quantum 
theory of solids. In the later part of the course the discussion will be focused on the voltage current behavior of the 
devices. In the last part of the course, some special devices like solar cells, light emitting diodes etc. will be discussed. 
2. Scope and objective of the course: 
The objective of the course is to develop an understanding of the basic phenomenon of the semiconductor devices. 
The main content of the course is having theoretical description of these devices which is an essential requirement in 
order to understand the operational details of any device.

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
This course will discuss the physics behind the semiconductors and the devices. The structure of any solid material plays 
an important role in their operation; the discussion will start with basic crystal structures and will cover the quantum 
theory of solids. In the later part of the course the discussion will be focused on the voltage current behavior of the 
devices. In the last part of the course, some special devices like solar cells, light emitting diodes etc. will be discussed. 
2. Scope and objective of the course: 
The objective of the course is to develop an understanding of the basic phenomenon of the semiconductor devices. 
The main content of the course is having theoretical description of these devices which is an essential requirement in 
order to understand the operational details of any device.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: 
 
This course takes us from the study of oscillations to waves, and finally to the foundations of quantum mechanics, 
tracing a connected thread through classical and modern physics. 
 
We begin with an introduction to oscillations and the model of simple harmonic oscillations, damped and forced 
oscillations, leading to the phenomenon of resonance. We shall study coupled oscillators : normal modes and 
frequencies, and the continuum limit of a large number of coupled oscillators. We will study transverse vibrations of 
a stretched string, the one-dimensional wave equation, and traveling wave solutions to the wave equation. We shall 
study energy transport in waves and pulses on a string, and their interaction with a boundary: reflection and refraction. 
Wave phenomena, such as the interference of light waves from two coherent sources, will lead us to wave -particle 
duality, the concept of t he photon, the de Broglie hypothesis, and matter waves. We shall study the Heisenberg 
uncertainty principle, the Schrödinger equation, and the wavefunction. We shall study the quantum problem of a 
particle in a one-dimensional box, energy quantization, barrier tunneling, the transmission coefficient, and introduce 
scanning tunneling microscopy as an application of quantum tunneling. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course:   
● Understand oscillatory motion:  Analyze simple harmonic motion, superposition of oscillations, and the 
effects of damping and external driving forces, including resonance and quality factor 
 
● Master the physics of coupled systems and waves: Explain how coupled oscillators lead to normal modes, 
and how taking the continuum limit gives rise to wave phenomena, including the wave equation, traveling 
waves, and energy transport 
 
● Analyze wave behavior and propagation:  Distinguish between group and phase velocity, and describe how 
waves interact with boundaries and each other through reflection, refraction, and interference 
 
● Grasp the foundations of quantum mechanics: Explain wave-particle duality, the de Broglie hypothesis, and 
the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and apply the Schrödinger equation to determine wavefunctions and

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: Introduction to oscillations, simple harmonic motion, superposition of harmonic  
oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, resonance and quality factor: transverse and longitudinal  
waves, wave speed in a stretched string, wave equation in one dimension, traveling solutions to the wave  
equation, energy transport in waves, standing waves, travelling sound waves; Interference of light waves,  
introduction to diffraction; concept of photon, photoelectric effect, Compton scattering; wave-particle  
duality, de Broglie hypothesis and matter waves; 1D Quantum wave functions: properties and applications;  
Pauli’s exclusion principle and multielectrons atoms, introduction to X-rays and Lasers.
2. Scope & Objective of the Course : This course introduces the fundamental concepts of classical and  
quantum waves, beginning with simple harmonic motion as the basis of oscillatory phenomena and  
progressing through mechanical waves, sound, interference, and diffraction. It then explores the transition  
from classical to quantum physics by examining the wave-particle nature of light and matter, culminating in  
an elementary introduction to quantum wave functions and their applications to atomic systems, X-rays, and 
lasers. Designed for undergraduate students with a basic knowledge of calculus, the course emphasizes  
physical intuition, conceptual understanding, and qualitative reasoning over advanced mathematical  
formalism. Its objective is to provide a unified understanding of wave phenomena across classical and  
quantum physics, establish the conceptual foundations of modern physics, and prepare students for advanced 
courses in optics, quantum mechanics, condensed matter physics, and related disciplines.

names: understanding of what constitutes a supply chain
insights into the various key components

sources.text:
Instructor In-charge :  SRIKANTA ROUTROY  
    : Hitesh Sharma (RS) 
     
1. Scope & Objectives of the Course: 
The fundamentals of supply chain – concepts course is aimed at providing a solid grounding 
and understanding of what constitutes a supply chain, setting the stage for more advanced 
topics. The course provides students with the opportunity to get clarity and insights into the 
various key components and concepts of the supply chain. This course will assist in 
understanding Supply Chain Management (SCM) not as a technology but rather a business 
strategy tool for the companies trying to create competitive advantage in the market. 
The objectives of the course are mentioned below:  
• Attain familiarity with the fundamental concepts of the SCM and its use in organizations.  
• Understand the key components of the Supply Chain and the interrelationships. 
• Importance of supply chain in today’s business environment and the impact of 
Globalization. 
• Supply Chain emerging trends

sources.text:
5. Course Plan 
Topic Contents 
What is Supply Chain 
Management & how 
does it create Value? 
Describe the cycle and push/ pull view of a supply chain.  Identify the key supply 
chain decision phases. Goal of supply chain & impact of supply chain decision on the 
success of a firm 
Strategic Fit & Scope Achieving strategic fit is critical to a company’s overall success.  
Supply Chain Drivers

insights into the various key components

sources.text:
Instructor In-charge :  SRIKANTA ROUTROY  
    : Hitesh Sharma (RS) 
     
1. Scope & Objectives of the Course: 
The fundamentals of supply chain – concepts course is aimed at providing a solid grounding 
and understanding of what constitutes a supply chain, setting the stage for more advanced 
topics. The course provides students with the opportunity to get clarity and insights into the 
various key components and concepts of the supply chain. This course will assist in 
understanding Supply Chain Management (SCM) not as a technology but rather a business 
strategy tool for the companies trying to create competitive advantage in the market. 
The objectives of the course are mentioned below:  
• Attain familiarity with the fundamental concepts of the SCM and its use in organizations.  
• Understand the key components of the Supply Chain and the interrelationships. 
• Importance of supply chain in today’s business environment and the impact of 
Globalization. 
• Supply Chain emerging trends

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
Types of Manufacturing, Manufacturing, maintenance, quality and service operations management concepts. 
Manufacturing Management measures , Factory/plant performance,  Operations Improvement framework. 
Maintenance management, optimising maintenance costs; Improving asset lifecycle; Preventive maintenance; 
Total productive maintenance (TPM); Quality  management - practices and processes; Total quality 
management (TQM); Service Operations Management definition; Customer loyalty and satisfaction. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This course details the various aspects and emerging concepts of operations management as they relate to the 
manufacturing/production function, maintenance, quality, and service operations. It provides a detailed view 
of each of the above functions, including their strategic importance, operational aspects, and roles in the supply 
chain. The objectives of the course are mentioned below:   
• This course will give students an overview of the various components of manufacturing and 
maintenance management as practised on  the shop floor. The various kinds of manufacturing 
operations, the types of jobs performed, and the maintenance activities undertaken to ensure 
operational readiness and integration with other functions of the industry will be discussed . This will 
help one understand how the shop-floor execution and upkeep of resources (machines/equipment) are 
critical to the functioning of a coherent supply chain. 
• This will help the students to understand the importance of quality management. Explain the various 
quality management tools and techniqu es used in an organisation to ensure that quality products and 
services are produced.     
• This course will provide an overview of the service operations management. Customer service design, 
service operations and execution, and monitoring service delivery performance will be discussed.

sources.text:
1. Course Description:  
Supply chain network design; Supply chain Relationships; Freight  modes; Logistics planning; Shipment 
execution; Transportation  sourcing and procurement; Freight Billing and Payments; Omni -Channel 
Distribution; Global Trade Management (GTM);  Warehousing; RFID in supply chain; Warehouse Picking; 
Yard Management; Strategic Sourcing; Agreements, Supplier Management;  Supplier Risk Management, 
Spend Analysis and Optimization; AI and  use cases in procurement; Inventory management -Concepts and 
classifications; Types of Inventory Transactions; Managing Uncertainty; cost management; inventory control 
techniques; Product  genealogy traceability and recall management; Replenishment;  Material movements 
across facilities; CPFR concept; Project Based Supply Chain; Digital Technologies in SCM; Integration with 
other SCM systems. 
2. Scope and Objective of the Course: 
This course will give students a broad overview of the fundamental theories regarding various logistics 
functions and their overall management. With this course, students will be able to approach logistics 
management with a holistic view and understand, analyse, and coordinate various functions within a coherent 
supply chain framework.  
• This will help students understand the various components of procurement – sourcing, contracting, 
supplier management, qualification management, purchasing of direct and indirect mater ials, spend 
analysis, and its integration with other management systems/applications. 
• This will help explore the importance of inventory management, the key components involved, and 
the best practices that businesses can implement to improve their inventory management processes.

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
Course Description: Success in any organization —from the smallest corner store to the largest 
multinational corporation—requires the use of cost accounting concepts and practices. Cost accounting 
provides key data to managers for planning and controlling, as well as costing products, services, even 
customers. Cost accounting is one of very important managerial tool for business strategy and 
implementation. 
 
1. Scope & Objectives of the Course: 
This course focuses on how cost accounting helps managers make better decisions, as cost accountants 
are increasingly becoming integral members of their company’s decision-making teams. 
 
The objectives of the course are mentioned below: 
i.  This course will equip students with the knowledge and analytical skills required to apply 
management accounting tools and techniques for planning, decision making, cost control, 
and performance evaluation in organizations.

Course Title : Fundamentals of Nanoscience and Nanotechnology

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1.Course Description:
Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address  
critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This  
course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and  
nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this 
rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, 
their synthesis and properties, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical,  
electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics,  
medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed.  
The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale  
systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future  
directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered.
2.Scope and Objective of the Course:
The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview  
of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis 
of nanoparticles and nanostructures.
Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials  
and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights 
real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological  
domains.
This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical  
exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into  
advanced study or research in the field.

Course Title              :  Fundamentals of Solid-State Physics

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the fundamental concepts of 
solid-state physics with a particular emphasis on semiconductor materials and their applications. It covers 
crystal structures and defects, the quantum and statistical principles governing electron behavior in solids, the 
origin of energy bands, and the electronic properties of metals, semiconductors, and insulators. The course 
further introduces carrier transport mechanisms, including drift, diffusion, and the Hall effect, bef ore 
discussing the thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids. Throughout the course, the underlying 
physical principles are connected to modern semiconductor devices such as LEDs, solar cells, photodetectors, 
and sensors, providing students with the essential foundation required for advanced studies in materials 
science, condensed matter physics, and semiconductor technology. 
 
2. Scope & Objective of the Course: This course introduces the fundamental principles of solid-state physics 
that underpin the behavior of crystalline materials and modern semiconductor devices. It encompasses crystal 
structures, basic quantum and statistical concepts, electronic band theory, semiconductor physics, and the 
thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids, while emphasizing their relevance to contemporary 
electronic and optoelectronic technologies. The primary objective is to develop a clear understanding of the 
relationship between the atomic structure of solids and their physical properties, explain the quantum 
mechanical origin of electronic behavior in materials, introduce the principles governing charge transport in 
semiconductors, and establish the scientific foundation necessary for the study, analysis, and application of 
semiconductor materials and devices in advanced engineering and physics courses.

Course Title: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:
Software engineering is a discipline that allows us to apply engineering and computer science con-
cepts in the development and maintenance of reliable, usable, and dependable software. There
are several areas to focus on within software engineering, such as requirement specification, de-
sign, development, testing, maintenance and project management. Software development outside
of the classroom is a very complex process, mostly because real-world software is much larger
and more complex. The purpose of this course is to present software engineering as a body of
knowledge. The course is designed to present software engineering concepts and principles in
parallel with the software development life cycle.
2. Scope & Objective of the Course:
This course provides an ability to identify, formulate, and solve complex engineering problems by
applying principles of engineering, science, and mathematics. This also develops an ability to
function effectively in a team whose members together provide leadership, create a collaborative
and inclusive environment, establish goals, plan tasks, and meet objectives. In addition, this
course also facilitates an ability to develop and conduct appropriate experimentation, analyze and
interpret data, and use engineering judgment to draw conclusions

9. Make-up Policy:
•Mid-Sem Exam has one make-up. This means, that a student can abstain herself/himself (on valid
reasons) in this Test. This make up would be conducted immediately after regular mid-sem exam and
would include complete syllabus. Of course, the student would apply for the make up in advance with
documentary proof.
•Only on producing documentary proof of possible absence, which proves that student would be phys-
ically unable to appear for the test/exam, the decision of granting the make-up will be taken.
•Prior Permission of AGSRD is required to get make-up for the comprehensive exam.
Tanmaya Mahapatra

Course Title: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING AND MANAGEMENT

syllabus.heading: Course Description

sources.text:
1. Course Description:
Software engineering is a discipline that allows us to apply engineering and computer science con-
cepts in the development and maintenance of reliable, usable, and dependable software. There
are several areas to focus on within software engineering, such as requirement specification, de-
sign, development, testing, maintenance and project management. Software development outside
of the classroom is a very complex process, mostly because real-world software is much larger
and more complex. The purpose of this course is to present software engineering as a body of
knowledge. The course is designed to present software engineering concepts and principles in
parallel with the software development life cycle.
2. Scope & Objective of the Course:
This course provides an ability to identify, formulate, and solve complex engineering problems by
applying principles of engineering, science, and mathematics. This also develops an ability to
function effectively in a team whose members together provide leadership, create a collaborative
and inclusive environment, establish goals, plan tasks, and meet objectives. In addition, this
course also facilitates an ability to develop and conduct appropriate experimentation, analyze and
interpret data, and use engineering judgment to draw conclusions
